bio.en: Shaun Clowes is Chief Product Officer at Confluent, previously CPO at MuleSoft (a billion-dollar business within Salesforce), CPO at Metromile, and a six-year Atlassian veteran who built the first-ever B2B growth team and created two popular Reforge courses.
bio.zh: Shaun Clowes 是 Confluent 的首席产品官（CPO），此前曾任 MuleSoft（Salesforce 内部一家十亿美元级企业）的 CPO、Metromile 的 CPO，并在 Atlassian 任职六年，打造了史上首个 B2B 增长团队，还创建了两门广受欢迎的 Reforge 课程。

summary.en: Shaun combines tactical execution with strategic framing, sharing lessons from building retention/engagement and data-for-PMs courses and leading product at multiple enterprises. He discusses how to think about retention and engagement as systems, the role of data in product decisions, and how to operate effectively as a CPO across very different company stages. The episode is packed with frameworks for product leaders scaling complex B2B businesses.
summary.zh: Shaun 将战术执行与战略框架相结合，分享了他在打造“留存/参与”与“面向 PM 的数据”课程、并在多家企业领导产品中的经验。他讨论了如何将留存与参与视为系统、数据在产品决策中的作用，以及作为 CPO 如何在不同阶段的公司中有效运作。本期为正在规模化复杂 B2B 业务的产品领导者，提供了满满的框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you have very strong opinion about this, which is just the state of the product management career and how most PMs are not that great.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你对此有非常鲜明的见解——这正是产品管理职业现状的真实写照，以及大多数产品经理表现平平的原因。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Why is it that product management is still such a relatively undeveloped discipline? We're like 15 to 20 years into this, and so there's something about the current state of product management that isn't getting at the truly important things, the truly value-added things. If we were doctors, you'd be like, "That's totally unacceptable."
turns.zh: 为什么产品管理至今仍是一个相对不成熟的学科？我们已经发展了15到20年，但产品管理的现状始终未能触及真正重要、真正能创造价值的核心要素。如果我们是医生，人们肯定会说：“这完全不可接受。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the answer, Shaun? How do we solve this problem?
turns.zh: 肖恩，解决之道是什么？我们该如何破解这个难题？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: In everything always talk from the customer's perspective, from the market's perspective, from the competitor's perspective, the very small number of PMs do that. They get dragged into internal politics, they get dragged into scrum management or scrum execution or product delivery, and you just can't win that way.
turns.zh: 在任何事情上，都要始终从客户视角、市场视角、竞争对手视角出发。能做到这一点的产品经理少之又少。他们深陷内部政治斗争，纠缠于Scrum管理、Scrum执行或产品交付等琐事，这样根本无法取胜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You kind of have this hot take that the way AI will most impact product management is data management.
turns.zh: 你曾提出一个激进观点——人工智能对产品管理影响最大的方式将是数据管理。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Well, you've got this synthesis machine, which is this LLM thing that's going to help you do synthesis, but if it hasn't got all that data to do synthesis on top of, it's got nothing. And so that means that LLMs can only be as good as the data they are given and how recent that data is.
turns.zh: 嗯，有一种合成引擎，比如LLM技术，它能帮助你进行数据合成，但如果没有足够的数据可供合成，那它就毫无用武之地。这意味着LLM的表现上限取决于所提供数据的质量和时效性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the future, if you can easily clone a B2B SaaS app like Salesforce or Atlassian, what happens to these businesses long-term? Do they just become, are they all in trouble?
turns.zh: 未来，如果像Salesforce或Atlassian这样的B2B SaaS应用能被轻松克隆，这些企业长期来看会面临怎样的处境？它们会陷入困境吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: People really underestimate where the value is created in these applications and they just kind of get it completely wrong.
turns.zh: 人们严重低估了这些应用的价值创造点，他们的理解完全偏离了正确方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny

You just talk about what you've seen there and you're just thinking here.
turns.zh: 首先，我想谈谈我深信不疑的一点——我很高兴你对此也有强烈的见解，那就是产品管理职业的现状。大多数产品经理表现不佳，而提升他们的能力有着巨大的空间。你可以分享你所见到的例子，也可以畅想未来。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, it's honestly a big conundrum for me. I think it's actually part of... It's grandiose to say so, a bit of my life's work. Why is it that product management is still such a relatively undeveloped discipline? We're 15 to 20 years into this thing. You would've thought that it would be less random than it is. The outcomes are random, the behaviors are random, individual performance is random, seemingly. And so there's something about the current state of product management that isn't getting at the truly important things, the truly value-added things, the right way to think about problems, the right way to think through problems, the abstract reasoning that's needed, there's something that isn't working about it. I spent a long time trying to put my finger on it and then be like, "How do you reproducibly reproduce that?" Reproducibly produce people who can really be really great product managers. (00:06:39): The thing is that if you think all the way back to it, I spent a long time as an engineer and people always talk about 10 times engineers and I wanted to be a 10 times engineer. I'll leave it to others to decide to tell you whether or not I was or I wasn't, but certainly I wanted to be and I tried to be a really great engineer. And it must be true that if there's 10 times engineers, and I would argue they definitely are, they must be 10 times product managers too. But at the same time, those 10 times product managers, because product management is ultimately about leverage, so it's about helping other people have dramatically more impact than they would if they were unorganized that they didn't have somebody to organize the goals and what we're trying to achieve, then that means that a 10 times product manager has 100 times return or more because they're 10 timesing the return on 10 times resources. (00:07:23): So the outcomes are so wild, like wildly distributed and the benefits are so good that you would've thought that it would've behooved us. There would've been a way that this had evolved and improved and really gotten way crisper than it has, but here we are. I'm not saying that we haven't gotten better, we 100% have, but I think we could all say that we're not reliably producing 10 times product managers every day of the week.
turns.zh: 说实话，这对我来说是个大难题。说句不谦虚的话，这甚至可以说是我毕生致力于解决的难题。为什么产品管理至今仍是一个相对不成熟的学科？我们已经探索了15到20年了，本以为它应该会比现在更有章法。结果却依然充满随机性——项目成果随机、团队行为随机、个人表现随机。似乎现有产品管理体系并没有触及到真正重要的部分，比如创造价值的思维方式、问题的正确解析、抽象推理能力等。这里存在着根本性缺失。我花了很长时间试图找到症结所在，并思考如何通过可复制的方式培养出真正优秀的产品经理。（00:06:39）回想起来，自己曾长期从事工程师工作，人们常说要成为“10倍工程师”，我也曾渴望成为10倍工程师。至于我是否达成目标，留给别人评判吧，但我确实想成为一名优秀的工程师。既然10倍工程师存在（我坚信他们确实存在），那么10倍产品经理也应该存在才对。但与此同时，10倍产品经理毕竟是关于杠杆效应的——他们能帮助团队发挥出远超个体能力的价值。所以，10倍产品经理的价值应该是100倍甚至更多，因为他们能用10倍资源创造10倍的回报。（00:07:23）结果却极其不稳定，收益也参差不齐。明明有如此丰厚的回报潜力，我们本应早该看到这个领域快速进化和完善。但现实却令人失望。虽然我们确实有所进步，但距离可靠地培养出10倍产品经理还有很长的路要走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this point and it's especially painful that when someone works with a PM that's not great. There's just this meme of why do I need PMs? PMs are useless, PMs suck, and it just creates that no one's ever like, "Engineers are useless or designers are useless." But there's so many people are like, "I don't need product managers on our team. Never hire a PM," and it just sets the whole profession back.
turns.zh: 我特别认同这一点，但当遇到不称职的产品经理时，那种滋味更是苦不堪言。网上总有那种调侃“产品经理有啥用？产品经理就是个废物”的梗，但人们从不说“工程师没用”、“设计师没用”。相反，很多人会说“我们团队不需要产品经理，永远别招产品经理”，结果整个行业都因此受累。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: When I first started out in PM somebody, it's obviously a chestnut, but he pointed out that realistically when you're a product manager, your job is to say no to 90% of things that get brought your way. And so that kind of makes you the bad person pretty much from the start. And so you're saying no to 90%, so you can say yes to 10% and that kind of puts you behind the eight-ball right at the very beginning, and so you have to very quickly get runs on the board. You have to prove to have the right insights, to have the right data, to make the right decisions or you don't get another go, you don't get another swing at it. So it makes sense that product managers are the easiest to single out and criticize, but that is also what makes it the funnest thing. (00:08:52): If you think about why do we do this? Somebody once asked me, "Would you retire? Why do people do what they do?" Because certainly at some point it isn't just about the money and at the end of the day product management is so damn fun because it's about trying to figure out an edge. It's like trying to look at the world, find the portion of the chessboard that isn't occupied, but that is valuable and find a way to get into it, invade it and destroy it. It's decisions under uncertainty and that makes it unbelievably fun. Really, really painful and very frustrating and very hard to convince people, but very, very fun. So in equal measures basically.
turns.zh: 我刚入行产品经理时，老大曾说过一句经典话：现实情况下，产品经理的职责就是对90%的需求说不。从一开始，你就注定是个“坏人”。当你否定90%提案时，剩下的10%才能说yes。但这种局面一开始就让你陷入被动局面——你必须迅速证明自己的洞察力、数据分析能力和决策力，不然就再也没有翻盘的机会。所以产品经理最容易被针对和批评，这也是这个职业最有趣的地方。（00:08:52）：你想过为什么我们要做这份工作吗？有人问我：“你会退休吗？为什么人们要做自己现在做的事？”因为终有一刻，钱不是唯一的动力。产品经理的乐趣在于不断寻找突破边界的机会。就像观察棋盘，寻找那些未被占据却价值千金的区域，设法占领并颠覆它。这是充满不确定性的决策过程，既令人痛苦又充满挑战，但确实无比过瘾。说到底，乐趣与挑战是并存的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the answer, Shaun? How do we solve this problem? I know you said it's your life's work. What do you find actually helps most in helping PMs level up and become say 10 X PMs?
turns.zh: 肖恩，解决之道是什么？你说这是一生的追求。具体来说，哪些方法最能帮助产品经理提升能力，实现10倍成长？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: I think the most important thing and the chestnut that I repeat to everybody is that at the end of the day, the time you spend looking inside the building doesn't really benefit you very much at all. And Steve Blanken, people used to talk about you should be spending 80% of your time thinking about things going on outside the building. You might not be outside the building, but you should spend 80% of your time thinking outside the building. And I would say that very small number of PMs do that. They get dragged into internal politics, they get dragged into scrum management or scrum execution or product delivery, like elements of the delivery thing and you just can't win that way. You just can't win that way. You can never get an A because you're fundamentally not solving the job. The job is not about execution or anything, it's about finding reliable, differentiated value that you can uniquely deliver into the market. (00:10:33): So I would say if there's one thing, two things I would say actually that I generally guide product managers to do, one is to always start from the point of view outside the building in every document in everything, always talk from the customer's perspective, from the market's perspective, from the competitor's perspective, and the people who listen to me on that I would say get better almost immediately because they're starting from a place that's easier to understand and then secondarily be data informed. (00:10:58): They use all of that view of the world, but don't just make up a bunch of statements, support that statements with anecdotes and bits of data. It doesn't have to be a treatise, but convince everybody of what the world really looks like and what the opportunities ahead of the company looks like and good things happen to you. And all of a sudden you go from a world where nobody wants to help you get anything done to where everybody wants you to win. They want you to win and they may not give you everything you want, but they certainly will try because they're like, "Well, of all the bets we could make, this is a good one."
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的一点，也是我反复告诫所有人的道理，那就是归根结底，你花在内部事务上的时间并不会真正为你带来多大益处。史蒂夫·布兰肯曾说过，你应该把80%的时间用于思考公司外部的事务。即便你身处公司内部，也应该把80%的时间用于思考外部市场。实际上，很少有产品经理能做到这一点。他们会深陷内部政治斗争、Scrum管理或产品交付等事务中，但这样做注定不会成功。你永远无法获得高分，因为你根本没有解决核心问题。产品经理的工作重点不是执行细节，而是要找到可靠且差异化的价值，并将其独特地推向市场。（00:10:33）所以我要说，有两件事是我通常指导产品经理去做的。首先，在每份文件和每个决策中，都要始终从外部视角出发——从客户视角、市场视角、竞争对手视角出发去思考。我发现那些听从我建议的人往往能迅速进步，因为他们从更易理解的视角出发。其次，要用数据说话。（00:10:58）他们要充分利用这种外部视角，但不要随意下结论——要用案例和数据来支撑观点。不必写成学术论文，但要让所有人相信现实世界的模样，以及公司未来机遇的图景。这样一来，你就能从无人相助的困境中走出，迎来众人助你成功的局面。虽然他们未必能满足你所有要求，但至少会尽力相助，因为他们会想：“在我们能做的所有选择中，这个方案堪称良策。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine many people listening to this are thinking, "Oh, I am that person. I talk to customers all the time. I'm always interacting, looking at research, putting data together." And what you're saying is you're probably not doing that enough. Is there anything that you could help someone recognize of, "No, you're actually not doing this enough and you think you are but you're not."
turns.zh: 我想很多听众会说：“哦，我就是那种人。我们总是和客户沟通，不断研究数据，整合信息。”但你说这可能还不够。你能否帮助人们意识到：“不，你做得还不够。你自以为做得多，但实际上远远不够。”

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: It's one thing to say you're spending a lot of time looking outside the building. It's a whole other thing to hear from the places you don't normally hear from. So avoid availability or confirmation bias. Most of the time people go talk to the people they always talk to and they learn nothing particularly new. They don't synthesize the results that they got from that conversation. They don't seek out the counterfactual, they don't seek out the proof that they're wrong. They don't analyze what their competitors are doing and figure out what that must tell you about the market. They don't bring back the data of how their product is actually being used versus how people say it's being used. It's like all data and no analysis is not very useful. Everyone can bring back an omnibus edition of random stuff I heard on a Tuesday, but the competitive advantage is extracted out of figuring out what other people don't see, figuring out where we are wrong, figuring out where a well-placed bet could have dramatically outlandish returns. (00:12:49): And so I think firstly, people often say that they do a lot of this stuff, but they actually don't because they don't have any structured way of doing it. So what they really mean is every now and then I get in a customer call or every now and then I get stuck into an escalation. And so they're kind of conveniently bucketing it. So firstly they don't do it in a very structured way, then they don't bring back analysis, they get true insights from that thing, so they don't really gain very much at all. It's just more activity, no outcomes. People do far too much activity with not enough outcomes and there just isn't enough time in the day to do that to be successful.
turns.zh: 光是说你花了很多时间观察外部环境是一回事，但从那些你平时不常接触的渠道获取信息则完全是另一回事。因此，要避免可得性偏差和确认偏差。大多数时候，人们只会去和那些他们常交流的人交谈，却学不到什么新东西。他们不去综合分析对话中获得的结果，不去探寻相反的观点，不去验证自己可能存在的错误，也不去分析竞争对手的动向，进而洞察市场趋势。他们不去核实产品实际使用情况与用户口述使用情况的差异。就像只有数据而无分析是毫无用处的。任何人都能随口讲出一堆周二听到的零碎信息，但真正的竞争优势在于发现别人看不到的东西，认识到自己的错误所在，洞察到一项明智决策可能带来极高回报的机会。（00:12:49）所以我认为首先，人们常说自己做了很多这类工作，但实际上并未做到，因为他们缺乏系统的操作方法。他们真正想说的是偶尔接到客户电话，偶尔处理升级事务，然后把这些归为“临时应付”。所以首先，他们缺乏系统的操作流程，其次无法从中提取真正的洞察，最终根本无法获得实质性收益。这不过是徒劳的忙碌，毫无成果。人们投入过多精力却收获甚微，一天根本没有足够的时间来取得成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You as a product leader is at the Venn diagram center of the sweet spot of where this podcast has been going recently, which is product and growth and how AI helps you with all these things. And so to follow a thread there with synthesizing and understanding what people are saying, user research and surveys and all these things, have you found any tools that you and your team have found really useful to help you do this more efficiently versus traditionally just manually going through all the stuff and finding patterns?
turns.zh: 作为产品负责人，您正处于本期播客核心探讨领域的交汇点——产品与增长，以及AI如何助力实现这些目标。延续这个主题，谈到综合分析用户反馈、用户研究、调查等内容，您和团队是否发现了哪些高效工具，能比传统手动筛选数据、寻找规律更高效地完成这些工作？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, so firstly, stepping back a little bit just into the motherhood and apple pie portion of qualitative research or whatever, I find that most people don't even understand or don't start with a rigorous foundation in what they're going to need to do to get the answers that they want. So for example, your listeners have probably heard about the Nielsen number before, but basically the idea is that once you interview between 7 and 14 people, you stop learning new things. Less than 7, you don't learn enough, more than 14, you start learning anything new. And so if you interviewed two people, you probably don't have enough data. If you interviewed 22, you probably had too much, so they don't even right size their efforts. So that's a problem. So they don't start that way. Then they go into these conversations asking leading questions, which really are designed to get the customer to say what they already want to be true, which is so they haven't done enough research or they've done too much and then they've blown up all of the results before they've even heard anything. (00:14:48): If you don't right size your research and you don't set this up to learn, then you're going to lose. No amounts of applying LLMs or any type of kind of structured reasoning is going to help you. Because you just basically you're reading back what you want to hear or some weird summarized version of what you want to hear. But stepping back from all of that, what I like to do specifically getting to LLMs is I think that we live in just the most amazing time for product managers right now in terms of being able to analyze vast quantities of information and see the common threads. And so let me give you few examples of that. One might be you can do a bunch of customer interviews, you can put a bunch of customer interviews into ChatGPT and you can say, "Hey, ChatGPT, this is my strategy. Tell me where my strategy does not fit what these customers talked about." (00:15:40): It's all about the not, not where it does, where it does not. People spend far too much time looking for what they're hoping to see, not for what they're not looking to see. So you can literally ask ChatGPT to help you find where the customer is probing at the edges of what you're trying to do, where it's wrong, where what you're saying is not what they believe. And you can ask it questions like that. You can ask it what your customers are saying would better fit what your competitors are saying. So you can basically say, you can copy and paste one of your competitor's positioning documents into ChatGPT and say, "Is this a better fit for what they have said than my thing?" Which is you can summarize your own strategy, you can take your competitors but public documents and you can ask it to summarize what their strategy probably is. (00:16:22): And it's actually supposedly good at that because mostly your public documents are actually a summary or at least they're derivative of what your strategy is. So it will give you crazy insights into what other people's, literally their product strategy at times creepy like, "Oh, they will probably do this, they will probably do that. It's more likely they would do this than they would do that." And so normally that type of insight was hard one, it took a lot of sweat work. You basically get to read a lot of stuff. You kind of had to use your brain as this big summarization machine and eventually you knew what you felt about all the things you had read, but you couldn't summarize why. LLMs let you get to that really, really, really quickly in a very structured way, but only if you push at the edges, provoke the answers you don't want to hear, provoke the problems, try and prove to yourself that you are wrong, I think is the easiest way to start trying to use some of these tools.
turns.zh:
是的，首先，退一步讲，回到定性研究中关于"母性本能"之类的部分，我发现大多数人甚至不理解，或者没有从严谨的基础开始规划如何获取想要的答案。比如，你的听众可能听说过尼尔森法则，但核心观点是，一旦你采访7到14个人，就无法再获取新信息了。少于7人，信息不足；超过14人，信息过载。所以如果你只采访了2个人，那数据量肯定不够；如果采访了22个人，又可能信息过剩。因此，他们甚至没有合理规划研究规模。这就是个问题。他们从一开始就没做好准备。接着，他们在访谈中抛出引导性问题，引导客户说出他们希望成立的观点——要么是因为研究不足，要么是因为信息过载，结果还没听完，就把所有结果搞砸了。（00:14:48）：如果你没有合理规划研究，没有明确学习目标，那注定会失败。再多的LLM应用或结构化推理都无济于事，因为你最终得到的只是重复自己想听的内容，或者是某种奇怪的总结版本。退一步讲，具体到LLM应用，我认为当下对产品经理来说，正是最激动人心的时代——能够分析海量信息并发现共性规律。让我举几个例子：你可以对大量客户访谈进行处理，输入ChatGPT，问它："嘿，ChatGPT，这就是我的策略。告诉我我的策略与客户提到的内容不符之处。"（00:15:40）：关键在于"不符"而非"符合"。人们往往过度关注希望看到的结果，而忽视不想看到的信息。因此，你可以让ChatGPT帮你发现客户在挑战你的策略边界、指出错误之处，或者指出你的说法与客户信念不符。例如，你可以把竞争对手的定位文档复制到ChatGPT，问它："这比我的策略更符合他们的定位吗？"你可以总结自己的策略，再拿竞争对手的公开文件，让它总结他们的策略。（00:16:22）：据说ChatGPT在这方面很擅长，因为公开文件通常是策略的总结或衍生版本。因此，它能为你提供惊人的洞察，比如竞争对手可能采取的策略，哪些更可能，哪些更不可能。传统上这类洞察需要耗费大量心血——你得阅读大量资料，用大脑当作总结机器，最终形成自己的理解，但无法解释原因。LLM能让你极快地获得这些洞察，效率极高。
以一种结构化的方式，但只有当你突破常规，触及那些你不愿听到的答案，挑起那些你不愿面对的问题，试图向自己证明自己是错的，我认为这才是开始尝试运用这些工具的最简单方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And it sounds like in your experience you're just using straight-up OpenAI, ChatGPT, Claude, not any specific tool for user research for this specific use case.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这一点。在你的经验中，你似乎只是直接使用OpenAI、ChatGPT、Claude等工具，而没有针对这个特定用例专门开发用户研究工具。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: No, mostly I find that the straight-up LLMs themselves are good enough and we do have some internal tooling that we built around, I don't know if you've ever had Sachin Rekhi on the show, you may have. He was a product leader pretty well known in the gross community, and he was a leader at LinkedIn for a long time and he used to call this concept a Feedback River, and he basically said that really smart product managers are constantly swimming at a Feedback River. They set out to surround themselves by Feedback River and I really deeply believe in that. It's like, "Okay, how can I surround myself with user interview data, with direct customer feedback, with NPS data, with competitor information?" Like I'm always trying to wash myself over with information. And where I'm going with this is that LLMs and tooling based on it can be exceptionally good for this. (00:18:20): So for example, at Confluent we get a ton of inbound customer requests, as you can imagine coming from the field or directly from customers. We use LLMs to take in those asks to summarize what they're about, to find other asks that are like that one, really in a compelling way, a real way, like a semantic way, not other words, exactly the same, are these the same concept? So that we can look across all of the inbound demand on us and say, "Well, the most popular idea is this one and is getting more popular. The least popular idea is this one. It is getting less popular." In a really deep rich way, even across hundreds or thousands of pieces of inbound feedback. I think it's a really great time to be a product manager if you can put these types of tools to work, but they don't do the job for you, they just help you do these things that are intricate in that job of finding the gaps, finding the opportunities, finding the common threads without necessarily having to do all of it just inside your wear-wear, just inside your brain.
turns.zh: 不，我发现直接的LLM本身就足够好了。我们内部也开发了一些相关工具。你可能听过Sachin Rekhi来过我们的节目吧。他是产品界知名人物，曾在LinkedIn担任高管。他把这种理念称为"反馈河"，意思是真正聪明的产品经理会持续在反馈河中游泳。他们致力于让自己被反馈河环绕，我对此深信不疑。比如，"如何获取用户访谈数据、直接客户反馈、NPS数据、竞争对手信息？"我总是在努力用海量信息武装自己。这就是我要说的，LLM及其相关工具在这方面能带来极大助力。（00:18:20）比如，在Confluent，我们会收到大量客户请求，来自一线或直接来自客户。你知道的，我们用LLM来处理这些请求，提炼其核心需求，寻找相似请求，真正以一种有意义的方式——语义层面而非字面层面——识别重复内容。比如，"这个想法最受欢迎且日益流行"，"这个想法最不受欢迎且日益冷落"。通过这种深度分析，我们能在数百甚至数千条反馈中洞察趋势。若能善用这类工具，产品经理的黄金时代已然到来，但工具并不能替代你的工作，它们只是辅助你完成那些复杂任务——发现空白、捕捉机遇、梳理共性，而无需闭门造车、冥思苦想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to stay in this AI river that we're in right now and ask a couple more AI-related questions. And this may be what you just said, but I'm curious if there's more here. You kind of have this hot take that the way AI will most impact product management is data management and data versus models you're building or anything else. Can you talk about what you've seen there?
turns.zh: 接下来我想继续探讨AI领域，问几个相关问题。你可能已经提到了这一点，但我想深入了解一下。你认为AI对产品管理影响最大的是数据管理，而非模型构建或其他方面。你能谈谈这方面的见解吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I think there's two implications for people as they're building products based on AI and as they're thinking about AI in their workflow. So let's start with the first one, because that's how product managers do product management things. You just asked this question of should it be specific tools built to make AI easier for product managers to use? Or is it in fact more general models being put to work? At the end of the day, these models are very, very, very smart, but they're also insanely dumb and everyone knows that, insanely dumb. In other words, they really only know what they were trained on or what you bring to them right at that moment. In that millisecond, and then they will forget it immediately. And it's very easy to convince yourself that isn't true, but it is actually what really matters. And let me add one extra piece that makes that really important. (00:20:28): At the end of the day, information has a decay rate. So think about customer feedback, it has a decay rate or what your competitors are doing has a decay rate. So any new piece of data decays in its value to your decision-making very, very quickly, very, very quickly. You can plot your own decay chart if you want to, but the answer is very, very quickly. And so when you think about the job which is synthesizing all of this very complicated information to make good decisions, what does that mean? Well, you've got this synthesis machine, which is this LLM thing that's going to help you do synthesis, but if it hasn't got all that data to do synthesis on top of, it's got nothing. And so that means that LLMs can only be as good as the data they are given and how recent that data is. They're ultimately like information shredders. (00:21:11): They are limitless information eaters. You can never have enough information to give to an LLM to truly gain its value. The more things you give it, the better it gets. Broadly speaking, that's just not perfect, but that's close enough. And so what that means is as an internal product leader or putting LLMs to work, you need to figure out how to bring as much information about customers or their asks or your competitors, all of it. How much can you find all of it and bring it together and give it to the LLM either in your tooling or even in just copying and pasting or whatever your flow is going to be, that's one thing. But then if you take it beyond that and you go, "Okay, well now I'm a product leader and I'm building an app and I want to put AI in my app, what will make my AI experience really great?" (00:21:57): It's definitely not going to be the models because these models are mostly going to be somewhat replaceable. And you could say, "Okay, well, is it going to be the prompts?" Maybe, but certainly good prompts are better than others, and that's kind of an ongoing investment you'd probably want to make to ask better questions to get the LLM to deliver better answers. But it's obvious that the real answer is the context, all the context you're going to give it, all the data you're going to copy and paste. And so if you think about, let's say I'm building a, I have no relationship to this, but let's say I was trying to build a human capital like a HCM bot, like an AI bot. Let's say I was working at Workday and I was trying to bring an AI bot. It's pretty obvious that the smarts of the bot would really be related to all of the employee information, but not just that, it would be the benefit's information, it would be the legal situation in the country where that person is currently working. (00:22:47): It would be the company's policies and procedures that apply to it. So you get what I mean, by about these kind of the jumps of logic and the jumps of data and the way data is all linked together. If you want to have a smart AI experience, you'll convince yourself that all I really need to do is get a model and wire it in and I'll build a little pipeline that will suck some data in and it will whack it into the LLM. And if you think that way, you're going to be very sad, very, very sad for a very long time because you are constantly going to be wrestling with how do I get data to this thing? How do I get good data to this thing? How do we get timely data to this thing? How do I get well-structured data to this thing? (00:23:21): And so it's a data management problem. It's getting access to good data, getting access to high quality data, getting access to timely data and getting it to the LLM to get the LLM to make a smart decision. That's where 90% of the calories go. Maybe it's a bit like Einstein's thing, "It's 10% inspiration, 90% perspiration." Nobody wants to hear it. Everybody wants to just think about what these really cool models and how smart they are, and the next one will be even smarter. But really it's just the hard work of getting really good data to the LLMs to get them to do good things.
turns.zh:
是的，我的意思是，当人们基于人工智能开发产品，或在工作流程中考虑人工智能时，有两个关键启示。先从第一个说起，因为这正是产品经理进行产品管理的核心所在。你刚才提到的这个问题——是否应该开发专门的工具来让产品经理更轻松地使用人工智能？还是说应该采用更通用的模型？归根结底，这些模型非常、非常、非常智能，但它们也极其愚蠢——所有人都知道这一点，极其愚蠢。换句话说，它们只会记住训练过的内容，或是你当下提供的信息。在那一瞬间，它们能理解这些信息，但转眼间就会遗忘。这很让人难以置信，但这才是关键所在。让我再补充一点至关重要的内容。（00:20:28）：归根结底，信息是有衰减率的。想想客户反馈，它有衰减率；竞争对手的动态也有衰减率。因此，任何新数据对决策的价值衰减都极其迅速，极其迅速。你可以自己画个衰减曲线图，但答案就是——衰减速度极快。所以当你思考如何综合这些复杂信息来做出正确决策时，这意味着什么？你有这台综合机器，也就是LLM模型，它能帮助你完成综合工作。但如果没有足够的数据可供综合，它就一无是处。这意味着LLM模型的表现取决于所提供数据的质量和时效性。它们最终就像信息粉碎机。（00:21:11）：它们是无底限的信息吞噬者。你永远无法为LLM提供足够的信息来真正发挥其价值。你提供的信息越多，它的表现就越好。但说实话，这并不完美，但已经足够接近了。因此，作为内部产品负责人或将LLM应用于实际工作的人，你需要想办法收集尽可能多的客户信息、竞争对手动态以及所有相关数据。无论是通过工具整合，还是直接复制粘贴等流程，这都是关键一步。但如果更进一步，你会问：“好的，我现在是产品负责人，我要在应用中加入AI功能，怎样才能让AI体验真正出色？”（00:21:57）：答案肯定不是模型，因为这些模型大多可以被替代。你可能会说：“那是不是用提示词呢？” 或许可以，但优质的提示词确实比普通的要好，这需要持续投入，帮助LLM获得更好的回答。但显而易见，真正的关键在于上下文——你提供的所有信息、数据复制粘贴的所有内容。比如，我假设我在开发一个与Workday相关的HCM机器人应用。很显然，机器人的智能程度将取决于所有员工信息，但不仅如此，还要考虑福利政策信息，以及该员工当前所在国家的法律法规。（00:22:47）：
这些都属于公司适用的政策和程序。所以你应该能明白我的意思——关于逻辑跳跃、数据衔接以及数据整合方式。如果你想获得智能AI体验，就会误以为只需获取一个模型、将其集成进系统，再搭建一个小型数据管道，将数据导入LLM即可。但如果你这样想，那你注定会大失所望，长期陷入困境，因为你总要纠结于如何获取优质数据、如何确保数据及时性、如何构建结构化数据，以及如何将这些数据输入LLM以助其做出明智决策。这些问题才是核心所在，耗费了90%的精力。或许这就像爱因斯坦所说的"灵感占10%，汗水占90%"。没人愿意听这些道理，人人都只想畅想那些超酷的模型及其智能程度，而下一代模型还会更胜一筹。但说到底，关键在于为LLM提供优质数据，助其发挥真正的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds really obvious as you make this case. It makes me think about at the Lenny and Friends Summit, Mikey Krieger talked about how he had the two types of PM groups within Anthropic. One was focusing on user experience product and the other was working on the model research side, and they realized that all of the success came from the model research work, like making the model and the data they provided the model was where all the value came from, not just optimizing the user experience and they're just putting more and more of their product team on just that versus tweaking UX and buttons and things like that.
turns.zh: 听你这么说确实挺显而易见的。这让我想起在Lenny and Friends峰会上，Mikey Krieger谈到Anthropic内部有两类产品经理团队。一类专注于用户体验产品，另一类则致力于模型研究。他们发现所有成功都源于模型研究工作，比如模型构建以及为模型提供的数据才是核心价值所在，而非仅仅优化用户体验和调整按钮之类的表面功夫。因此，他们正将越来越多的产品团队资源投入到模型研发上，而不是在用户体验微调和界面美化上浪费精力。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, exactly right.
turns.zh: 对啊，说得太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something sort of related, I'm just going to ask one more AI question. I don't want every talk to end up being just all AI, but something that's kind of been a meme recently, and I know you have a perspective on this, is that AI makes it really easy to build products. So in the future, if you can easily clone, say, a B2B SaaS app like Salesforce or Atlassian or whatever your favorite B2B SaaS app, what happens to these businesses long-term? Do they just become, are they all in trouble? Are there going to be 100 Salesforce competitors? What's your sense and prediction on what might happen there?
turns.zh: 再说个相关话题。我想再问一个关于AI的疑问。我不想让每场演讲都围绕AI展开，但最近有个热议的话题，我知道你对此有独到见解，那就是AI让产品开发变得轻而易举。那么未来，如果能轻松克隆像Salesforce、Atlassian这类B2B SaaS应用，或者你最喜欢的B2B SaaS应用，长期来看这些企业会怎样？它们会被淘汰吗？会涌现出100个Salesforce的竞争对手吗？你对此有何看法和预测？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's really weird. I think people really underestimate where the value is created in these applications and they just kind of get it completely wrong, and I'm not sure why that is. So if you think you bet. So I spent a long time at Atlassian, so I worked a lot on Jira, which many people know, and I spent a long time at Salesforce, so I spent a lot of time in the CRM ecosystem, the marketing ecosystem and all the rest of it. If you want it to be not charitable, you'd step back and you'd look at all those applications and you'd say, "They're all just forms on databases." You'd say, "The Jira is a form on a database, Workday is form on a database, so Salesforce." They're all forms on databases, all vertical SaaS or business SaaS is ultimately forms on databases. And you're be like, "Well, how hard can that be to replicate?" (00:25:45): And the answer is unbelievably hard, unbelievably hard. And people just think, "You totally get it wrong." Because it's not actually just about the data model. So if you think about, if it formed some databases, it's these beautiful user experiences that sit on top of data models. So whatever the object is, it might be a customer object or a campaign object or an employee object, you could say that, "Well, there's some elements of lock-in in the object, the object itself, like the fields of the object." I'm like, "Pretty boring. That's not very interesting." But sure, maybe. Certainly there's some value in being the system of record like the default that everybody uses. There's definitely some value in the UX. Like, "Well, I want to be the best HR-facing applications for working employee data." Yeah, there's some value there, but the real thing just staring at everybody in the face is it's all about the business rules. (00:26:35): That is what drives the lock-in because why do you buy Workday? You don't buy Workday for its out-of-the-box configuration. You buy Workday because you want to configure it to be Lenny Inc's HR processes. It becomes Lenny Inc's Workday. It's not Shaun Inc's Workday, it's Lenny Inc's Workday. And actually the longer you have the software, the more it becomes that, the more it becomes less and less like Workday and more and more like your specific company. Which makes sense because it was built to be configured to meet the needs of any specific company, and every company is their own precious snowflake. And as that happens, those configuration pieces, the bit that makes the application native and a fit for your organization makes it a fit for nobody else's organization and also makes it a black box to the point that you don't even understand how it works anymore. (00:27:20): If you went to, for example, Salesforce and you said, "Hey, could you define all of the processes by which software was sold inside Salesforce?" They couldn't tell you that without reading the code of their Salesforce instance. That's not a proprietary secret. That's obviously true because over time, that's literally how sales happened. There is no other way to do a sale other than through their internal tooling. And so what that means is that it's not the UI that matters and it's not the data model that matters, although those are both very useful. It's the years and years and years of evolution of the underlying workflows of the product to support the customers, but also the customers evolving those workflows to make them work the way they do. And so how does that impact AI companies? You could say, "It's easier than ever to build forms on a database application." (00:28:09): And so I'm like, "Yeah, okay, that presumably drives the incremental value of every new one of those to zero, right?" So probably leads to more power to the existing winning systems of record because there'll just be a gazillion competitors who would just more form some databases. So like, "How would you ever choose between them? You may as well just go with the winner. Nobody ever gets fired for buying Salesforce or whatever. You may as well start from the kind of the premier vendor." That's one element. You could go the other way and you could say, "I've heard a few people mount this argument," which I think is really interesting that at the end of the day, agents are going to take away most of the use of that user interface. (00:28:44): So let's say for example, your Salesforce with Service Cloud, I've heard people say, "Well, a lot of those service agents might end up being replaced with agentic workflows. That will mean that there is no person operating the UI. If the UI doesn't even exist anymore, then why do you even need Salesforce? We may as well just have raw database tables on who even needs forms of databases, you can literally just have databases." But that also doesn't make any sense either because the agents have to operate against the rules of the system and the rules are defined by the business processes. So think about Salesforce without a head. Imagine Salesforce had no UI, it would still have those business rules that I was talking about. And those business rules are what define what the agent should do. They're almost telling the agent what it should do and how the world can operate, what is possible, what is allowed. And so from my perspective, this idea that this just completely destroys the differentiation of these kind of business process SaaS applications just seems like a fantasy, a crazy fantasy. (00:29:42): The only way I could really believe it is if you said, "Well, you could have a new startup that introspected all of the rules that are configured into a Salesforce to try and reverse engineer what your actual business processes are and then kind of operate on top of that." But the best place people to do that would be Salesforce themselves or Atlassian in Atlassian's case or Workday in Workday's case. I just can't see a world in which this... I think one of two things could happen. All this moving to AI makes those applications even better, even more unassailable, they basically get stronger. It makes us stronger or it could enable some new level of applications that come from a more platform based thing, so less a domain specific thing like you ACM or ERP or engineering or less of the domain specific stuff. (00:30:36): It could enable a more platform like play where you have more business objects and business objects have rules. And you could imagine a world in which there's kind of a whole evolution of new more platform like SaaS applications that do more than one business function worth of the business rules and the way things move around in the enterprise, but that doesn't exist today. So you could say that that could exist and it could say it could be way better than we've ever thought of because of AI. Or you could say that the rich are going to get richer. The most likely outcome is that the currently dominant companies are going to get more dominant, but I don't think this idea that it would just cause a spring up of a whole bunch of new apps that will more easily challenge the incumbents makes any particularly, it's not straightforward to me how that would happen basically.
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得这真的很奇怪。我觉得人们真的低估了这些应用程序中价值的创造方式，他们完全理解错了。我也不知道为什么会这样。我在Atlassian工作了很长时间，所以我对Jira有很多了解，很多人都知道Jira；我在Salesforce工作了很长时间，所以我在CRM生态系统、营销生态系统等领域花了很多时间。如果你不带有慈善心，退后一步看看所有这些应用程序，你会说，"它们不过是数据库上的表单。" 你会说，"Jira就是数据库上的表单，Workday也是数据库上的表单，Salesforce也是。" 它们都是数据库上的表单，所有垂直SaaS或商业SaaS最终都是数据库上的表单。你会想，"复制它能有多难？" （00:25:45）：但答案是难以置信地难。人们只是觉得，"你完全理解错了。" 因为这不仅仅是关于数据模型的。所以如果你考虑一下，如果它只是一些数据库，那么这些漂亮的用户体验就建立在数据模型之上。无论对象是什么，可能是客户对象、活动对象或员工对象，你可以说，"好吧，这个对象本身有一些锁定元素，比如对象的字段。" 我会说，"这太无聊了。这没什么意思。" 但当然，也许有一些价值。当然，作为默认的记录系统也很有价值，每个人都使用它。用户体验也很有价值。比如，"我想要成为面向人力资源的最佳应用程序，用于处理员工数据。" 是的，这里有一些价值，但真正摆在每个人面前的是商业规则。（00:26:35）：这就是驱动锁定的原因，因为你为什么购买Workday？你购买Workday不是为了它的开箱配置。你购买Workday是因为你想将其配置为符合Lenny公司的人力资源流程。它变成了Lenny公司的Workday。它不是Shaun公司的Workday，而是Lenny公司的Workday。实际上，使用该软件的时间越长，它就越变得越像Lenny公司的Workday，而越不像Workday本身。这是有道理的，因为它是为满足任何特定公司的需求而构建的，而每家公司都是独一无二的。随着这种情况发生，这些配置片段——使应用程序本地化并适合你的组织的部分——变得不适合任何其他组织，并且也变得像一个黑盒子，到最后你甚至不再理解它是如何工作的。（00:27:20）：如果你去Salesforce，例如，你说，"嘿，你能定义在Salesforce内部销售软件的所有流程吗？" 他们无法在不阅读Salesforce实例代码的情况下告诉你。这不是专有秘密。这显然是真的，因为随着时间的推移，这就是销售的实际方式。除了通过他们的内部工具，没有其他销售方式了。那么这对AI公司有什么影响呢？你可以说，"在数据库应用程序上构建表单比以往任何时候都更容易。" （00:28:09）：所以我觉得，
是啊，好吧，这很可能导致每款新产品的增量价值归零，对吧？所以这可能会让现有的主流系统集成商（SaaS）变得更强，因为会有无数的竞争对手涌入，充其量只是建立一些数据库。那么你会怎么选呢？你很可能会选择胜者通吃，毕竟没人会因为买了Salesforce之类的产品而被解雇。何不从头开始，选择顶级供应商呢？  

但反过来，或许有人会说：“我听过不少人这么说。”我觉得这很有意思——说到底，代理人最终会接管大部分用户界面操作。（00:28:44）比如说，Salesforce结合Service Cloud，我听有人说：“很多客服代理可能会被代理式工作流取代。这意味着没有人操作UI了。如果UI都不存在了，那还要Salesforce干嘛？我们大可以直接用原始的数据库表格。” 但这同样站不住脚，因为代理人必须遵循系统规则，而这些规则是由业务流程定义的。想象一个没有UI的Salesforce，它仍然会有我提到的那些业务规则。这些规则决定了代理人该做什么，指导着业务运作，规定了什么是可能的，什么是被允许的。在我看来，这种认为SaaS应用会被彻底淘汰的观点简直是痴人说梦。  

（00:29:42）唯一能让我相信这种说法的，或许是有人说：“可以让新创公司解析Salesforce中的所有配置规则，逆向工程出实际的业务流程，然后在此基础上进行开发。” 但最适合做这件事的应该是Salesforce本身、Atlassian或者Workday。我实在无法想象这种情况会发生。我认为有两种可能：要么AI让这些应用更强大，更加牢不可破；要么它能催生出基于平台的新型应用，摆脱ACM、ERP、工程等领域的专有逻辑。  

（00:30:36）它可能会支持一个基于平台的生态系统，拥有更多业务对象，每个对象都附带规则。可以想象，未来会涌现出一批全新的平台型SaaS应用，这些应用能整合多个业务功能，整合企业中的业务规则和数据流转。但目前这种情况并不存在。所以要么这些应用会变得比我们想象的更出色，要么就是巨头会变得更强大。最可能的结果是现有巨头会进一步巩固地位，但我不认为会有大量新应用迅速挑战现有巨头，这种设想在我看来太牵强了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that was extremely fascinating and there's so much there. I can go in so many directions. One is I thought you would actually go in this direction, which is distribution advantages become even more important if it's easy to... Like today, I could sit there and hire team clone. Salesforce might take a while, but I could copy it, but by the time I'm done, they've evolved, they're moving, they're adding features, they're ahead, right? You're skating to where the puck was. And so if that's the case, one of the advantages, one of the ways to get anywhere is to have some kind of distribution advantage. It's one thing to have Salesforce as a product clone, another to get anyone to know about it, to adopt it, to sell it, procurement, all that stuff. Do you have a sense of distribution advantages being even more valuable in that world?
turns.zh: 哇，这真是太引人入胜了，内容实在太丰富了。我可以从多个角度展开探讨。首先，我原本以为你们会朝着这个方向发展——即若能轻松复制现有产品，分销优势便会变得更为关键。就拿今天来说，我可以坐在这里复制Salesforce的模式，但等我完成复制时，Salesforce可能已经在不断升级、增添新功能，始终保持领先。对吧？这就像是追随市场的脚步。既然如此，获取分销优势就成了达成目标的关键之一。将Salesforce产品进行复制是一回事，但要让用户知晓并采用它、进行销售、完成采购等环节，则是另一回事。你觉得在这种环境下，分销优势是否会变得更加珍贵？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, it certainly makes sense. Ultimately, at the end of the day, distribution is always an advantage because the hardest problem is to even be in the consideration set for any given problem. The world is full of problems. It's just when people have that problem, they firstly don't think they're going to solve it at all. And when they do think of solving it, they don't think of you. So distribution is always an incredible advantage. But again, in the world of AI, it seems like distribution is more likely to get hard than easy. So if you think about, for example, diminishing returns on cold email because cold email is getting easier and easier to send even worse spam, it sounds better, but it's effectively causing everybody to become desensitized to everything. I don't know if you've noticed, half the LinkedIn charts now are all basically clearly LLM generated spam. (00:32:50): I mean, to some degree it's actually worsening the signal-to-noise ratio. And so I think that a lot of the breakthrough distribution mechanisms that startups often use seem to be getting more crowded just in general and more expensive. That doesn't bode well for, "I'm the not as good Salesforce," "I'm the not as good Salesforce, but I'm cheaper." It has to be something different. There has to be some angle upon which you are materially better. And what I saw happening and what I've been seeing happening, and I think it's been really interesting is a lot of modern next-gen applications bringing data as a first-class citizen into the workflow. And I think that that's pretty compelling. So if you look at the next-generation of applicant management products that deal with inbound job applicants, a lot of them now like the latest core ones, they include your time to fill data, they include outcome data of who's got the best hiring outcomes, who over what period of time has the worst attrition, literally all the way back to the interviewers and where the interviews were in the interview cycle. (00:33:58): So basically embeds data into the whole life cycle. So I think that there are these ways in which startups can bring these experience benefits by just bringing a different approach to the world that does enable them to capitalize on traditional disruptive innovation. At the end of the day, this is just disruptive innovation. It means that most companies have overshot the utility like the average utility, so you can win by meeting the average utility and being different, meet the bar and be different. Meet the bar and be different is the way to cut through. So that makes sense if that's a half decent playbook. But even for those companies, now they're going to have all these AI competitors who are using AI to engineer faster, to build a competitor just like them as quickly as possible and start jamming it into the channel. And it's going to be interesting to see how this whole thing evolves. It kind of got race to the bottom characteristics around it. You're probably right, the distribution is still the hardest part in software, particularly when you're getting started.

是啊，我觉得说到底，关键在于以上所有因素，对吧？如果你拥有第一方数据却无法有效利用，那就没什么用处了。如果你掌握了第三方数据并能以有趣的方式加以应用，问题在于数据无处不在。数据充斥着我们的生活。真正重要的是在正确的时间、正确的地点获取正确的数据，因为我们都是普通人。所以在我看来，数据固然有其优势，甚至能形成网络效应——如果你能掌控极具价值的第一方数据，那更是锦上添花。但归根结底，关键在于能在正确的时间、正确的地点为用户提供正确的数据，让他们从中获益。（00:36:48）：顺便说一句，我职业生涯中有很多这样的经历。说来奇怪，我做产品经理很久了，但最后总是不由自主地接手数据团队。事实上，我在不同公司管理过多个数据团队，这挺奇怪的，因为产品经理通常不负责数据团队。我想我对数据有一种天生的亲近感。我曾自诩为数据驱动型人士，这曾是我的专长。但事后回想，我意识到数据其实恰恰相反。数据更像是指南针，而非 GPS。如果把数据视为提供答案的工具，那你注定会出错。要么出错，要么行动迟缓。要么出错，要么行动迟缓，有时两者兼而有之，因为数据大多不会直接给出答案。它只是告诉你，你刚刚提出的观点是否荒谬，或者某个方向是否存在可能性。
（00:37:44）：所以关键在于质疑自己的假设，避免行动迟缓。如果试图将数据用于所有场景，你的大脑最终会变成数据筛选器之类的。所以你的直觉之所以会告诉你某件事，是因为你见过大量数据，这些数据告诉你这很可能是最可能的答案。因此，数据驱动、痴迷于数据，是一种极易走向极端的倾向。所以关键在于适度使用数据，掌握触手可及的正确数据，形成正确的数据观，而不是期望数据能提供答案，或将其作为武器，或试图用数据迫使他人认同你的观点或跟随你的方向。但数据是万物的核心，关乎如何影响和成功打造产品、内部争取支持等方方面面。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: I think the first thing I always encourage people to do is to look at a piece of data. If you're looking at a piece of data and the result tells you something that your intuition tells you is insanely wrong, like they probably not right. First, believe your intuition and go and prove yourself right. Don't just take it at first glance because most of the time it's like Occam's razor. The most likely explanation for something that is insanely not intuitive is that it's just wrong, that there's a problem somewhere. Now, occasionally, sometimes you actually will be right. Now those will be paid dirt moments. Those are the moments that make it all worth it. There are times when you do find the negative goal, you're like, you're staring at it and like, "This is it. This was the problem. This was the thing we were looking for this whole time." (00:40:18): But you have to be very diligent about following it through, really understanding what you're looking at. Is this data representative? Is this data a good sample of the audience we care about? Is it already subject to some sort of selection bias? Oftentimes when I see analysis from different product leaders or even data teams, you can drive a truck through it, literally drive a truck through it. And if you present data with authority and that data is ridiculous or the analysis is just full of holes, you don't just not get benefit for that. You lose a whole bunch of brownie points. It would be better not to show up with an analysis that isn't clear than it would be to show up with an analysis that's dumb. And I see people self emulate on this actually relatively regularly because they just bring a knife to a gunfight or whatever, they did bring in an analysis that is just not, it doesn't hold water and they present it and then get shot down live, which is nobody's idea of a good time. (00:41:21): So if I give you a little bit of additional tactical things about that, it'd be okay if I'm looking at a piece of data, what was upstream of this piece of data and does that look normal? So this thing happened or whatever, which you're very, very excited about, what happened before that? And does that match what you think should have been right? So what happened before this momentous situation? And then, okay, for that thing that you're looking at, what happened after? If you have an idea of what happened before and after, that gives you some idea of whether or not this thing, is it all worth interesting to talk about? And then go one click above this data that you're looking at. So it's like, these things, let's say I'm looking at onboarding success. Let's say I'm looking at onboarding success to second week retention or something like that. (00:42:05): I'm like, "I have found this thing that totally crushes it. This intervention crushes it." If you go upstream and you find out that this intervention only applies to 2% of the inbound onboarding stream, it's meaningless. It's most likely just a random aberration. But even if it was not a random aberration, it's not a useful tool. And so you've got to go up and then you might go downstream and you might find, yep, they last for two in the second week, but in the third week they all churn. They're basically pointless. Why are we even talking about this? Or then you might step all the way back and go, "Okay, yes, those people do get retained for longer, but their average ASP is smaller." Because what we really care about, we do care about engagement and we care about more customers, but we want to keep the customers at a high ASP to reach a certain revenue goal. (00:42:46): The final goal is happy customers paying us money. So that's what I mean about going a click up. If you go a click to the left, a click to the right, so before and after and then a click up and you still see the thing that tells you the story that you want to tell, then now you've got something that's very compelling because people want to hear about that. They want to hear, "Well, what did happen before? What did happen after? And why is that outcome happening?" But you have to really do your homework and really be rigorous about it to avoid fighting fool's gold.
turns.zh:
我认为我首先要鼓励大家做的一件事，就是仔细审视数据。如果你看到的数据结果与你的直觉判断严重不符，比如看起来明显错误，那很可能存在问题。首先要相信自己的直觉，然后去验证。不要轻易下结论，因为很多时候这就像奥卡姆剃刀原理——最显而易见的解释往往是错误的。偶尔你确实能猜对，但这种情况往往转瞬即逝。真正值得庆幸的时刻，是当你发现负面结果时，那种豁然开朗的感觉——“原来问题在这里，我们一直找错方向了！”（00:40:18）  

但你必须非常严谨地追踪数据，确保其代表性和样本性。数据是否有偏差？是否符合目标受众的特征？是否存在选择性偏差？我经常看到产品负责人或数据团队提交的分析报告，漏洞百出，专业性堪忧。用错误的数据做分析不仅无益，反而会损害你的公信力。与其展示模糊不清的分析，不如保持专业素养。  

（00:41:21）  
所以我想给出一些实用的建议：  
首先，分析数据前要了解其上游数据是否正常。比如你对某个关键事件兴奋不已，但其前置条件是否合理？其次，要追溯下游结果，确认因果关系是否成立。  

举例说明：  
假设你研究的是新用户转化率，发现某个干预措施效果显著。但当你深入研究发现，该干预仅适用于2%的入站用户流，这就失去了实际意义。即使不是随机波动，也无法推广。  

再比如，分析第二周用户留存率时，发现某个指标异常高。但追溯上游数据发现，该指标仅在2%用户中出现，说明数据异常。即便真实有效，也不具备普适性。  

最后，退一步审视整体数据，发现虽然转化率提升，但用户生命周期价值却下降。这时你才意识到，整个分析方向可能存在根本性错误。
收入目标。（00:42:46）：最终目标是让满意的客户向我们支付费用。这就是我所说的"向上再迈一步"的意思。如果你向左或向右各迈一步，查看前后对比，然后再向上深挖，最终呈现的故事依然引人入胜，因为人们想听其中的来龙去脉。他们想知道"之前发生了什么？之后又发生了什么？为什么会出现这样的结果？"但你必须做好充分准备，保持严谨性，避免追逐虚幻的成功。

turns.zh: 真有意思。我们上次做类似的事情时，实际上有一个全球性的保留组，所有实验都不针对这个组。实验平台根本无法定位这个组。所以10%的人从未看到任何实验结果。这真的非常有用，因为你可以将他们与同一批次的其他实验组进行对比。我同意你的观点。但另外，我不太喜欢某些常见的思维模式。比如，“如果一个实验显示出暂时的益处，但这种益处无法持久，这是否意味着这个暂时的益处根本不值得追求？还是说这只是一个达成更高水平的机遇，而你只是没有抓住？”我认为没有一个完美的答案。这就是我想说的。我不认为一个益处无法持久就意味着你失败了。但我同意你的观点，即不去理解净收益或提升幅度也非常重要。这就是增长如此困难的原因。增长是产品的重要组成部分，尤其是在产品层面。
