turns.zh: 是的。是啊，这让我感觉自己老了，但确实，那是很久以前的事了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Slash maybe it's a new thing.
turns.zh: 或许这现在已经是新事物了。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's either a long time ago or it's just recently figured out this is a thing that you could do in a B2B is focus on growth.
turns.zh: 无论是很久以前，还是最近才意识到，这在B2B领域是一件值得关注的事情——那就是专注于增长。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, it is. So that was around about 2012, and at that time growth hacking was a thing. People don't really use that term anymore, but in B2C it was a very big deal because people could see Facebook doing their 10 friends in seven days and they could see this kind of thing that was working for people. And they're like, "Man, that's amazing." And at Atlassian we set out to go, "Okay, well, do those techniques work in B2B?" And also, it's kind of obvious now that a lot of them do and that it's worth doing. But at the time it wasn't that obvious because for a lot of B2B companies, I mean, you summarized it earlier, Lenny, distribution covers all faults. Almost all ills can be filled in by really great distribution. (00:46:52): If you have a really good marketing, a really good ground game, and you're kind of jamming your product into the channel, you're jamming your product in front of people and you're papering over the ugly parts with customer success people and services and consulting and whatever, that people will buy almost any software or you can certainly be successful with a lot of different software. But back in 2012, it wasn't clear of like, okay, which instead you went at this differently and you've heard them in software that sell itself, is the juice worth the squeeze? And now I would say that it's pretty clear that the juice is worth the squeeze to the point that lots of think about this all the time, but it was a bit of an interesting time at that time.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。大约在2012年，增长黑客策略风靡一时。虽然现在人们不常用这个术语了，但在B2C领域，它曾引发轰动，因为人们看到Facebook在七天内就吸引了10个好友，类似的成功案例层出不穷。人们感叹道："天哪，这太神奇了。"在Atlassian，我们开始思考："好吧，这些策略在B2B领域是否同样适用？"如今看来显然很多方法确实有效，值得尝试。但当时这并不明显，因为对许多B2B公司而言，正如你之前总结的，分销几乎可以解决所有问题。几乎所有问题都可以通过出色的分销来解决。（00:46:52）：如果你有出色的营销、扎实的基层工作，将产品强行推入渠道，让人们看到产品，再用客户成功团队、服务和咨询等手段掩盖产品的不足，几乎任何软件都能卖出去，或者说很多软件都能成功。但在2012年，人们还不清楚该如何突破常规。你听说过那些能自动销售的软件吗？但现在我可以说，这绝对值得投入精力去探索。虽然当时很多人对此心存疑虑，但现在看来成果显著，许多人都在深思这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that was essentially the beginnings of product-led growth. Is that a simple way to think about it?
turns.zh: 这基本上就是产品主导增长的开端。这么理解对吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Basically it's now called PLG, but yeah, at that time we didn't even know what to call it exactly.
turns.zh: 现在通常称之为PLG，但当时我们甚至不知道该怎么准确命名。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just growth. So based on that experience, a lot of B2B companies now have growth teams through investing in growth, what makes a great growth team in B2B? Any pitfalls you often find folks fall into that you think they should try to avoid?
turns.zh: 就是专注于增长。基于这段经历，现在许多B2B公司通过投资增长团队来推动增长，如何打造一支优秀的B2B增长团队？你认为人们常犯哪些错误需要避免？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Ultimately, a lot of these types of endeavors are a matter of balance. So what I mean by that is growth teams tend to go through a set of phases. Their first phase is proving their value at all. So call that the gold rush phase. This thing's probably not worth even doing. Why are we doing this, merry band of people out there trying to prove that there's some growth effect somewhere? So that's the proof of phase. And so the advantage of that phase is life's good because there's usually a lot of growths to be found because nobody's gone looking before, so life's good. But it's pretty random because you're just literally searching across a random search phase going, "Have we tried X? Have we tried Y? Have we tried Z?" Then once you get that model going, then it starts to be, "Okay, how do we scale this thing? Is this just a flash in the pan? Do we just find a little bit of low hanging fruit and there's nothing else here, there? Is this just a project we should have done rather than an ongoing thing?" (00:48:52): So you have to make it a system. You have to prove that it can be repeated, and then you have to scale it. It has to become a thing. It has to become part of your DNA. You have to be taking a PLG lens to everything you do, all the way from paid acquisition to activation, retention, engagement, cross product expansion, upsells, I mean, you name it, all the different ways you can grow a product by revenue or engagement. There's many different ways to go about that. And so you end up having to scale out and be able to do all of those different things. And then you have to figure out how you fit in with the rest of the organization because there's other people who build products all day every day. (00:49:27): There's other people who sell that product all day, all day. There's other people who market that product all day, all day. And so growth organizations are in this interesting space, they're in between everybody else. They're in everybody else's sandpit in a little bit, in a little way, and they're kind of at the edge of everybody's full-time job and they are very valuable, but they can be complicated because of all those relationships, and because of the way they sit amongst all of the other parts of the organization. So many organizations fail because they don't really find much the wins or when they do find wins, it just seems totally random. Or they do find a lot of wins, but they all can't understand them because they seem like they're just a random walk through a bunch of potential opportunities. There's many different ways to fail to fit as you go through your growth phase from trying the ideas to success, to scaling, to operationalizing.
turns.zh: 归根结底，许多这类努力都需要平衡。我所说的平衡是指，增长团队往往会经历几个阶段。第一个阶段是证明自身价值。可以称之为"淘金热阶段"。在这个阶段，事情可能根本不值得去做。我们为什么要做这件事呢？一群热衷于证明某处存在增长效应的人们。这就是证明阶段。这一阶段的优势在于，生活充满机遇，因为之前无人探索过，所以机遇唾手可得。但这种机遇也极具随机性——你只能在随机探索阶段不断尝试："我们试过X了吗？试过Y了吗？试过Z了吗？"一旦模式建立后，问题就转向："如何扩展这个模式？这只是一时兴起吗？我们是否只是抓住了低垂的果实，而其他地方毫无建树？这只是一项临时项目，还是持续的业务？"（00:48:52）因此，你必须将其制度化。必须证明其可重复性，然后进行扩展。它必须成为体系的一部分，成为你DNA的一部分。你必须将增长思维贯穿于整个业务流程，从付费获客到激活、留存、互动、跨产品扩展、追加销售等——只要能通过收入或用户参与度来增长产品，都可以尝试。实现增长的方式多种多样。最终你需要实现规模化并能胜任所有相关工作。然后，你还需找到与其他部门的协同点，因为其他人每天都在专注于产品研发、销售、市场推广等工作。增长团队处于一个微妙的处境，他们介于各部门之间，部分触及其他人的核心职责，处于每个人的全职工作边缘。这类团队极具价值，但也容易陷入复杂的利益纠葛之中。许多组织之所以失败，要么是未能找到明确的成功路径，要么是即使取得了成果，也因看似随机而迷失方向。要么是成功案例层出不穷，但其他人却无法理解其背后的逻辑，因为这些成功似乎只是在一堆潜在机会中随机探索的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the biggest memes along these lines is a lot of companies claim there's like just PLG rarely ever works. You always, either you try it and it just doesn't work or it eventually just peters out, I guess. Any thoughts on just what are signs that your product has a chance to work, peel product-led growth versus just go straight to sales immediately and don't even worry about this?
turns.zh: 在这类讨论中，最常见的观点是许多公司声称产品主导增长（PLG）模式很少奏效。要么尝试后失败，要么最终逐渐式微。关于如何判断产品是否有成功的机会，以及如何区分产品主导增长与直接销售模式，有什么见解吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: First let's examine the counterfactual, right? So let's start with the opposite of your question and say, "Hey, how would the world be sadder if we all just gave up on PLG?" We just said, "Hey, there's no point in doing it in B2B SaaS." The problem is that there is not a natural force that pulls companies towards thinking about the end user's enjoyment and success early in their journey. There is no natural force, there's no natural kind of a link force. Why is that? I mean, 101, the buyer is the most important person. The economic bar is the most economic person. Their needs are the number one thing. They're usually the person driving the RFP. They're usually the person dealing with the sales organization. So the needs of the person who you hear are usually all feature-driven and they're not from the end users. (00:51:34): And so you're kind of sowing a seed of your own demise if you don't think about that end user. But it's one thing to say that you should think about the end user, it's a whole other thing to have a system by which you do that because people pay lip service to all sorts of things. But I'm sure you've heard this one before, but in economics, people only do what their incentives told them to do. Broadly speaking, that is what they do, that is what happens. You get what you set out to measure. You get what you give people incentives to do. If there is nobody in the organization whose true incentive is to measure their end user success, their enjoyment, their happiness, their retention, their engagement early on, it will not happen. Or at best it will be a hobby. And so then by extension, if I start from there, then I say, "Okay, let's say it doesn't exist, PLG doesn't exist and therefore it's a hobby and therefore there will be a bunch of hobby people who care about this." (00:52:23): Then you ask yourself, "Okay, will that mean that there will be many products for which those experiences really suck? And does that mean that that will be an opportunity for competitors of those products to be better at that? And is that a differentiated competitive advantage?" Yeah, I'd say it is. I'd say it is. And so I just work my way backwards and I go, "Okay, you can say that your PLG investment might be too high." You could be like, "Well, if I invest more, I won't get any more juice. I can't spend my life just experimenting in the onboarding. That's not the only thing that matters." And that's very, very true, but it's very hard to argue it should be turned to zero. (00:52:59): And so to me, therefore it's about the balance. It's about, "Okay, how does PLG fit with the other different ways that I grow in my business?" At Confluent, for example, we have a PLG function. We do grow with self-serve signups. People who sign up, literally their credit card, lots of them sign up and they're very successful, never speak to us. We also have an enterprise sales team that sells directly to very big companies, some of the biggest banks in the world, the people you would definitely know of. I don't think it has to be one or the other. I think that it's about a balance. It's about getting the motions to work and for really sophisticated companies, the people who really nail this, it's about making both motions work together. If you can get a PLG motion work to feed your sales team and a sales team motion work to feed your PLG funnel when the sales leads aren't ready yet and you can get those motions into playing with each other, you can make a lot of money. (00:53:52): It can be an extremely successful way to go to build a very resilient business. Why? Because you get a lot of customers and you get a lot of revenue. You can't be that successful as a company if you have a lot of revenue, but a small number of customers because you're captive, everyone knows that. You can't be that successful as a company if you have a lot of customers, but not enough revenue because you shouldn't have enough money to sustain operations. So the magic is in having both, a very large number of customers and a very large amount of revenue, it's very hard to knock over a company like that. If I look back on my time at Atlassian, and I think that they shared their most recent numbers, I can't remember what it was, but it was in the public data or whatever, something 80,000 or 100,000 customers, something like that. (00:54:30): That's a lot of customers. That's a lot of customers. Let's say you're going up against Jira and you're like, "Yeah, man, I'm going to pick off 1,000 customers from Atlassian." That's a lot, right? That's a lot. Obviously 1,000 customers is a lot. You only have 19, sorry, it's going to be 89,000 to go or 79,000 to go, or however many it is to go. I can't remember their exact number of customers, but it's very hard to assail a company which has a very large number of customers and a very large amount of revenue. And so that's why I think that PLG as a mechanism is incredibly important for almost any type of company, if you can make the motion work. Obviously there are companies for whom the motion just isn't relevant, but for those where it does matter, it seems like the juice is worth the squeeze.
turns.zh:
首先，让我们来审视一下反事实假设，对吧？所以让我们从你问题的反面入手：“嘿，如果我们都放弃PLG，世界会变得更悲观吗？”我们刚刚说过：“嘿，在B2B SaaS领域这么做毫无意义。” 问题在于，没有一种自然的力量能促使公司在业务早期就去考虑终端用户的满意度和成功。没有天然的推动力，也没有自然形成的链接机制。为什么会这样呢？我的意思是，客户才是最重要的人。他们是经济价值的创造者。他们的需求是头等大事。他们通常是RFP的发起者，也是与销售团队打交道的人。然而，我们听到的需求往往都是以功能为导向的，而非源自终端用户。（00:51:34）如果你不考虑终端用户，那你就是在为自己的失败埋下种子。但说要考虑终端用户是一回事，但要建立起有效的体系则是另一回事。人们往往只是口头上说说而已。但我相信你以前也听过这个观点：在经济学中，人们只会做符合自身利益的事情。大体来说，人们就是这样行事的。你会得到你所衡量的东西，你会得到激励人们去做的事情。如果组织中没有人真正以衡量终端用户成功、满意度、留存率和参与度为己任，那么这些目标就无法实现。最多也只是个业余爱好。而由此延伸，如果我从这个角度出发，那么我会说：“好吧，就假设PLG不存在，因此它只是个业余爱好，那么就会有一群热衷于此的人。”（00:52:23）然后你会问自己：“好吧，这是否意味着会有很多产品提供的体验非常糟糕？这是否意味着这些产品的竞争对手有机会在这方面做得更好？这是否是一种差异化的竞争优势？”是的，我会说确实如此。因此，我会逆向推理：你可以说你的PLG投资可能过高了。你可能会说：“好吧，如果我投入更多资金，也无法获得更多回报。我不能把生命浪费在新用户引导上。这并非唯一重要的事情。” 这确实是事实，但很难主张应该将其完全舍弃。（00:52:59）对我来说，关键在于平衡。关键在于：“好吧，PLG如何与我业务增长的其他不同方式相契合？”以Confluent为例，我们有PLG功能。我们确实通过自助注册实现了增长。人们注册时，直接用信用卡付款，许多人注册后都非常成功，从不与我们联系。我们还有一个直接面向大型企业的销售团队，客户包括一些全球顶级银行，相信你肯定听说过。我认为不必非此即彼。关键在于找到平衡点。关键在于让两个动作协同运作。对于那些真正擅长此道的复杂公司而言，关键在于让两个动作相互促进。如果你能让PLG动作为销售团队提供线索，而销售团队动作又能为PLG漏斗注入线索——即使销售线索尚未准备好——并让这两个动作相互配合，你就能赚大钱。（00:53:52）这是一种极其成功的增长方式，可以打造出极具韧性的业务。
商业。为什么？因为你能获得大量客户和丰厚收入。若一家公司收入很高但客户数量很少，那它注定难成大业，因为用户锁定效应众所周知。同样，若客户众多但收入不足，公司也难以为继。所以关键在于两者兼得——海量客户与巨额收入。这样的公司几乎无可撼动。回顾我在Atlassian的经历，他们曾公开过最新数据，虽然具体数字记不清了，但公开数据显示他们有8万或10万客户之类的。（00:54:30）这就是庞大的客户基数。假设你要挑战Jira，你会说：“老兄，我要从Atlassian抢走1000个客户。”这数字听起来很诱人，但实际执行起来困难重重。毕竟Atlassian有19万客户（抱歉，应该是8.9万或7.9万，具体数字记不清了），要想撼动这样一个客户数量庞大、收入丰厚的巨头绝非易事。因此，我认为PLG（产品生命周期管理）作为一种商业模式对几乎所有公司都至关重要，前提是能让这个模式真正发挥作用。当然，有些公司根本不适用这个模式，但对那些适用的公司而言，付出努力绝对值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was an awesome answer. I looked up last year and they have 300,000 customers.
turns.zh: 太棒了，你的回答真精彩。我去查了一下去年数据，他们当时有30万客户。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Oh man, I'm so far off. When I left it must have been 80,000 customers.
turns.zh: 天哪，我差得太远了。我离开那家公司时，客户数量应该才8万吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They've done good work since then. Also, you're talking about incentives and how the power of incentives. Charlie Munger has this great quote I looked up just to make sure I get it right. "Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome."
turns.zh: 从那以后他们确实做得很棒。说到激励机制和激励的力量，查理·芒格有句名言，我特意查证了一下确保引用准确：“给我看激励措施，我就能告诉你结果如何。”

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, exactly right. I've seen cases where a sales team was people trying to get a sales team to do a PLG motion, and you can beat them over the head as much as you like, you can get into a meeting and tell them that you really, really want them to do this, but at the end of the day, they're not going to do it. And the same is true for every other kind of function. It's just the nature of things.
turns.zh: 是啊，太对了。我见过这样的情况：销售团队试图让成员推行PLG模式（产品导向销售），即便你反复强调、开会反复强调，告诉他们必须这么做，但最终他们还是不愿意执行。其他职能部门也一样。这就是人性使然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have some newsletter posts around the stuff of folks want to dig deeper. Also, Elena Verna had an awesome podcast episode talking about product-led sales and kind of the combination of these two things that we'll point to.. Just a whole other topic we can go deep, deep on, but we're not going to do that in this episode. Maybe just one more question. So you mentioned all the companies you worked at, so you've been at Salesforce, chief product officer, MuleSoft, specifically within Salesforce, Metromile, Atlassian, Confluent now, a lot of really interesting and different roles. How do you choose where to go work and how do you choose which opportunities to take? I imagine you have many options.
turns.zh: 我有一些通讯文章，感兴趣的朋友可以深入阅读。另外，埃琳娜·维尔纳（Elena Verna）在播客中深度探讨了产品主导销售模式，以及两者的结合，我们会重点推荐相关内容。这是个值得深入探讨的主题，但本期节目暂不展开。最后再问一个问题：你提到了曾任职的多家公司，包括Salesforce（担任首席产品官）、MuleSoft（在Salesforce内部任职）、Metromile、Atlassian和Confluent等，职位和职责都非常多样。你是如何选择工作机会和职位的？想必有很多选择吧？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: I have to think of my career. So in hindsight, looking at it this way, Lenny, so I don't know if forward-looking was obvious to me this way. But looking back, my career has been a little bit like a bingo card. I've always been looking to fill in boxes I didn't have filled because I felt like that would make me a better professional. It's like if I didn't know anything about that specific type of sales model or that type of marketing or that type of product management or that type of product or that layer in the stack or that kind of thing is like, well, if I learn about that thing, I will become more versatile. So actually two things, it's fun, it's fun to learn something new. It's fun to prove to yourself that you can do those new things and then it makes you more versatile because it means that any given problem you go up against, you've seen something that pattern matches to it. (00:57:29): It kind of feels like you end up bringing a gun to a knife fight in a way because every problem you look at, you're like, "Oh, I have seen this from the other side. I've seen this from some other angle, and so I know that this is likely to work and this is unlikely to work." And so when I joined early on in my career, I was working for a big enterprise software company, sorry, small enterprise software company that sold to the Fortune 100. When I joined Atlassian, and like I shared with you, we had no sales force at all actually at all. Literally nobody to sell the software. It sold itself or it didn't get sold at all. And we grew to have 80,000 customers. It was just pure product. They had growth and just an incredible company. Then it was at Metromile, which was a consumer company that got acquired, made an insurance product for end consumers. (00:58:13): So they got nothing to do with technology products, like literally a complicated Internet of things device you installed in your car, but ultimately it's an insurance product that you'd sell to grandmothers in Florida as much as you would ever millennials. And then at MuleSoft to totally back end software that's used by IT organizations and a consulate infrastructure that's used by developers everywhere to build really interesting data-driven applications, data powered applications to do all sorts of things in real-time. And you look at across all that and you go, "It's all a bit random." But I didn't see it that way because I learned, I actually was in sales for a bit, so I ran a pre-sales engineering group, went around the world selling software. So when I joined Atlassian, I wanted to kind of understand what it was to sell software at massive scale with no sales team, can it even be done? (00:59:01): And so I learned a lot in my time at Atlassian. When I went to Metromile, I'm like, "Well, I've never built a consumer product before." I can say that I've actually built a product that's touched many millions of people because Jira has, so I felt pretty good about that, but I'd never built one that I could say, "Yep, a consumer, your average consumer can use this thing. It's so simple. Even my grandma can use it." I'd never built a product like that. So I got that experience at Metromile, which is really fun. I'd never worked inside an organization as big as Salesforce or an organization with as good a sales motion. You talked about distribution earlier. Salesforce is an absolutely insane distribution machine, just an incredible company with just an amazing distribution network and a fantastic marketing approach that it's like a PhD in marketing. (00:59:44): When you spend your time at Salesforce, you're like, "This company is just one of a kind. It's a one of kind, and it's so outlandishly good at one specific thing." And so looking back, all of these jobs have been, when I say bingo card, I've just got an outlandish education in these areas that are not obvious at all. And once you've seen them, they're like superpowers. They're superpowers to be able to bring that same experience to bear on things. And so one thing that I really I'm trying to figure out is why often people don't do that. And oftentimes people stay in a very specific domain. They prefer to stay in a domain or they prefer to stay in a specific kind of type of company or a role that works in a certain way, like companies that have the same operating model or they plan the same way or they try to stay with things that are pretty similar. But it seems obvious that the most likely way to really grow is the opposite. (01:00:41): It's to constantly be choosing things that are either outside that, not totally outside the lines. Don't jump out of a plane if you've never parachuted before. Obviously you want them to be in some way and adjacency, that you want them to have something in common with what you know, but you want them to stretch you and change you. I had a really transformative experience many, many years ago when I was at Atlassian and a guy called Tom Kennedy, he was our general counsel, so chief legal officer basically, and a lifelong lawyer, very smart guy. I liked him very, very much. But just a lawyer. Just a lawyer, corporate lawyer, corporate counsel, I'm sure you know what they're like. And really great guy. And I remember, so mostly in our meetings he didn't talk that much except about legal things. But I remember in one meeting we were having this vigorous debate about a product strategy question about what we should do. Should we go left or should we go right? (01:01:39): And as usual, he's there and he's mostly just staying silent. And then eventually the conversation's been going on for 15 minutes and he is like, "Hey, everybody, a year ago we talked about X, Y and Z," and he proceeds to lay out our product strategy at that time, and he's like, "Just recently we said the following things, and that was a product strategy, whatever. Now you are saying this. Isn't it obvious that isn't this? What you guys are saying is not congruent with that, and if you really meant what you said back then we should be doing X." And again, the room went silent, everybody kind of turned to him, kind of nodded, and then everyone went, "Yeah, okay, I guess we probably should be doing it differently." And so the meeting stopped when the GCE randomly mentioned that he deeply understood our product strategy and he knew enough to be able to contribute in that way. (01:02:24): And so the life-changing part for me about that was just this realization that if I'm going to be a really great professional, the type of professional I want to be is that type of person. The type of person who can contribute to the whole company in all sorts of ways, doesn't spend all of their time in everybody else's business, but understands the business and has the mental horsepower and the experience to be dangerous in all sorts of, and I mean, that in a compliment way. I don't mean that in a negative way, but to be dangerous in all sorts of situations. I think that when you have leaders like that behind you and with you, then you're just unstoppable. You're an unstoppable force in business when you have that motion happening.
turns.zh:
我必须考虑自己的职业生涯。回过头来看，我觉得这事其实挺明显的。但当时我并不觉得自己有远见卓识。回首往事，我的职业生涯就像一张宾果卡。我总是在填补那些尚未填满的空格，因为我觉得这样能让我成为更出色的专业人士。比如，如果我对某种销售模式、营销策略、产品管理、产品本身，或者技术栈中的某个层级一无所知，我就会想，"只要我掌握了这些知识，就能变得更加多才多艺。"（00:57:29）这感觉有点像带着枪去参加刀战，因为面对任何问题，你都会想，"哦，我从另一角度看过这个问题，见过类似的模式，所以我知道这个方案很可能奏效，而那个方案则不太靠谱。" 我职业生涯早期曾在一家面向《财富》100强企业的企业软件公司工作（抱歉，应该是小型企业软件公司）。加入Atlassian时，正如我之前跟你们分享的，我们当时根本没有销售团队。字面意义上，根本没人负责软件销售。软件要么自己推广，要么就卖不出去。最终我们积累了8万名客户，靠的全是产品本身。他们发展迅速，是一家了不起的公司。之后我在Metromile工作，担任消费者业务公司，开发面向普通消费者的保险产品。（00:58:13）这与科技产品毫无关联，简直就是一个复杂的物联网设备，安装在用户车内，但最终还是一款面向佛罗里达州祖母们销售的保险产品，与千禧一代一样适用。再到MuleSoft，完全是后端软件，服务于IT组织和开发者社区的基础设施，用于构建实时数据驱动的应用程序。回首这一切，你会觉得很随机。但我当时并未意识到这一点，因为我不断学习。比如，我曾在销售部门工作，负责售前工程团队，全球推广软件。所以加入Atlassian时，我想了解如何在没有销售团队的情况下大规模销售软件，这真的能做到吗？（00:59:01）在Atlassian期间，我学到了很多。在Metromile，我意识到，"我从未打造过消费者产品。"我可以说Jira已经影响了数百万用户，但这与面向普通消费者、简单易用的产品完全不同。我在Metromile获得了这种乐趣。我从未在像Salesforce这样庞大的组织中工作，或者拥有如此出色的销售体系。你们之前提到的分销模式，Salesforce简直是个疯狂的分销机器，拥有令人惊叹的分销网络和卓越的营销策略，简直就是营销学的博士学位。（00:59:44）在Atlassian的时光让我收获颇丰。
销售云（Salesforce），你会说,"这家公司独一无二。它在某个特定领域表现得极其出色。"回顾过去，我从事的所有工作——我把它们比作"幸运抽奖卡"——都让我在那些看似毫不相干的领域获得了非凡的教育。这些领域一旦被你领悟，就堪称超能力。能将同样的经验应用于不同领域，本身就是一种超能力。但令人困惑的是，大多数人往往不愿这样做。他们宁愿深耕于某个特定领域，执着于特定类型的公司或角色模式——比如遵循相同的运营模式、规划路径、固守相似的框架。但显而易见，真正实现成长的路径恰恰相反。（01:00:41）关键在于不断选择那些虽不完全跳出固有框架，但又能带来新挑战的事物。比如从未跳伞过的人突然跳伞显然不明智。但这些选择必须与你的现有知识存在某种关联，既能激发你的潜力，又能推动你改变自我。多年前在Atlassian工作时，我有过一段深刻的蜕变经历。当时我们的总法律顾问汤姆·肯尼迪（Tom Kennedy）——一位资深律师、极具智慧且深受我尊敬的人——尽管身为律师，但他总能带来惊喜。在会议上，他除了谈论法律问题外鲜少发言。但我记得在一次关于产品战略的激烈辩论中，我们在"左派”还是“右派”之间犹豫不决。（01:01:39）通常他都保持沉默，但当讨论进行15分钟后，他突然说道："大家一年前讨论过X、Y和Z问题。"接着他详细阐述了当时的产品战略方针，并指出："而近期我们又提出了新策略。你们现在提的方案与之前的方向不符。如果你们真心践行了当时的承诺，现在应该采取X行动。"全场顿时陷入寂静，所有人都转向他，点头称是，随即达成共识："是的，我们确实应该调整策略。"会议之所以停滞，是因为GCE随口提及他对产品战略的深刻理解，足以为此贡献力量。（01:02:24）对我而言，改变命运的关键在于意识到：若想成为卓越的专业人士，我需要具备那种能从多方面为公司创造价值、既不事无大小插手他人事务，又能理解业务全局、具备思维敏捷度与丰富经验、能在各种情境中灵活应变的人才。拥有这样的领导者相伴，你将势不可挡。在商业战场上，你将成为一股不可阻挡的力量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that was an awesome story and an awesome perspective. It's similar to the advice I always give PMs of people always wondering, "Should I go deep on a specific subject? Should I just try different things?" And I find just variety, especially earlier in your career is really powerful, not just to help you discover the thing you like, but also to your point, just using insights from all these different parts of the product and internal tools and trust and safety and platform and consumer product side and growth and just core stuff. The more of that you have, the stronger you get. And I feel like another benefit of your approach is if you work at just B2B SaaS companies, if you have too many of that on your resume, it's very hard to get hired a consumer company. And so just having it creates a huge optionality for you if you do, which you did.
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个很棒的故事和很棒的观点。它和我的建议很相似——我总是告诉产品经理们，他们总在纠结：“我该深入研究某个特定领域吗？还是应该尝试不同的东西？” 我发现多样性真的很重要，尤其是在职业生涯早期。它不仅能帮助你发现自己真正热爱的东西，而且正如你所说，还能从产品、内部工具、信任与安全、平台、消费者产品、增长等各个不同领域汲取见解。这些见解积累得越多，你就会越强大。另外，我觉得你的方法还有一个好处——如果你只在B2B SaaS公司工作，在简历上堆积太多这类经历后，想进消费者公司就很难了。所以如果你能拥有多样化的经历，确实会为你打开更广阔的职业选择空间，而你显然已经做到了。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting because people used to talk about people who are T-shaped or whatever, and I've never really loved the analogy because it's more like people are scribble shaped. I mean, there's the really best people you've worked with, they're more like scribbles than they are T-shaped because of course you want to be horizontally capable, so you want to be broad and you do want to be deep, but you actually want to be deep in way more than one thing. Now obviously when I say deep, I don't mean I'm not able to do the job of our finance function all day every day, but I'm 100% good enough to go three clicks below the simple financial analysis. I can go reasonably deep in our financials because I want to and because it's partly it matters. It's important to be able to do that. And so maybe a different way to think about that bingo card is I've rarely regretted going deep in something that isn't quite my job. (01:04:51): I've rarely regretted it. The worst case scenario is I've learned something new that I will never use, which I guess at least that made my brain slightly more agile. I don't know, there must be some potential benefit of that. But the very best case scenario is that when I least suspect it at some point in the future it will turn out to be the thing that matters. It will be the tool that I need, but I'm facing some important problem and I will be like, "Oh my god, this was worth every cent." And so if you think about it on an ROI basis, doing things that aren't in your wheelhouse, that aren't the things directly in front of you, the ROI can really be outlandish. It can be off the charts great, but I guess it's speculative. Because you don't know you're going to need it tomorrow. You don't know if it's going to be something that's going to be a regular tool you use.
turns.zh: 是啊，这很有趣，因为人们过去常提到的T型人才之类的，我一直不太喜欢这个比喻，因为更像是乱涂乱画型人才。我的意思是，你合作过的最优秀的人，他们更像是乱涂乱画型的，而非T型人才，因为你当然希望具备横向能力，所以要涉猎广泛，但实际上你需要在多个领域深入钻研。当然，我说深入学习，并不意味着你能每天全天候处理财务部门的所有工作，但我完全有能力深入财务分析三层以下的内容。我能在财务方面做得相当深入，因为我愿意这么做，而且这确实很重要。那么，也许看待这张“宾果卡”的另一种方式是，我很少后悔深入研究某个并非直接职责范畴的内容。（01:04:51）：我很少后悔。最坏的情况是，我学到了永远用不到的新知识，但至少这能让我的大脑更灵活些。我不知道，这其中肯定有潜在的好处。但最好的情况是，当未来某个时刻你最意想不到的时候，这会成为至关重要的东西。它会成为你需要的工具，而你正面临某个重要问题时，你会感叹：“天哪，这真是物超所值。” 所以从投资回报率的角度来看，做那些不在你专长范围内的、不在你眼前的事，ROI可能会高得离谱。可能会好得超出想象，但这毕竟是投机行为。因为你不知道明天是否会用到它。你不知道它是否会成为你日常使用的常规工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting is the bingo card is the analogy. Is there a bingo moment at the end of this? Is there retirement?
turns.zh: 有意思的是，这张“宾果卡”就是个比喻。最后会有宾果时刻吗？会有退休时刻吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Oh, you mean you've got everything. You've got the collectible Pokemon?
turns.zh: 哦，你是说你已经集齐了所有元素？你收集了所有可收集的宝可梦？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, you collect them all.
turns.zh: 对啊，你把它们都收集齐了。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, I was working with somebody at Salesforce and he'd been there a long time, very, very, very successful person. Honestly didn't need to work anymore. And he said something that I found really useful. He's like, "Well, now I'm at the point of my life where I want to work at the intersection of things that I am good at and things that will be valuable to the company to do." So basically it feels like the reward of completing your Bingo card is actually to just get to spend more time doing things that are leverage, that you enjoy and that are high leverage. And so that seems like a good outcome to me. I don't think most people are going to work and hopefully have some sort of great financial outcome and then go, "Well, that's it. I'm picking up stumps, I'm retiring." I think for most people, achieving some sort of financial outcome or some sort of independence or whatever is really just another stage. At that point it will be, "Okay, well now what do I do? What do I do with my life?" (01:06:49): And so that was why I said earlier that at the end of the day, product management is at times the worst job in the world and at times easily the best. And it's both and it can be both. And so it's hard for me to think about if I think about the things that are the intersection of what I'm good at and are valuable to the world, product management is a pretty fun one to do and it's different every day. So I think we're pretty privileged. For those of you who listen, I mean, obviously your podcast reaches a lot of product people. I think we're pretty privileged to be able to operate at that intersection, but it's not easy because you got to show value. It's a very complicated job to show value in and to demonstrate value to the world, and it's constantly being attacked, like you mentioned, but it's still amazing when it all goes right. When a product is very successful in the market, it's hard to describe the joy you get from that.
turns.zh:
是啊，我之前在Salesforce和一个人共事，他在那儿待了很久，非常非常非常成功。说实话，他其实已经不需要再工作了。但他说了一句话，让我觉得特别有用。他说：“现在我的人生到了一个阶段，我想把自己擅长的事情和对公司有价值的事情结合起来。”所以基本上来说，完成Bingo卡的奖励，实际上就是能有更多时间去做那些能发挥杠杆作用、自己喜欢且高效益的事情。这对我来说似乎是个不错的结果。我觉得大多数人工作后，不太可能获得某种财务上的成功，然后就说：“好吧，就这样了。我收拾行李退休去吧。”我认为对大多数人来说，实现某种财务成果或某种独立性之类的，都只是另一个阶段。到了那个阶段，他们会问：“好吧，那接下来呢？我的人生该怎么过？” （01:06:49）  
这就是为什么我之前说过，归根结底，产品管理有时是世界上最糟糕的工作，有时又是最棒的。它两者皆是，可能两者兼有。所以当我思考那些我擅长且对世界有价值的事情时，产品管理就是一份相当有趣的工作，每天都不一样。所以我觉得我们很幸运。对于听众朋友们来说，我知道你们的播客覆盖了很多产品从业者。我们能在那个交叉点上工作真是件幸事，但这并不容易，因为你必须证明自己的价值。在这个领域展示价值、向世界证明价值是一项非常复杂的工作，而且它不断受到攻击，就像你提到的那样，但当一切顺利时，那种喜悦感简直难以言表。当一个产品在市场上大获成功时，那种喜悦是难以形容的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of along those lines to close out our conversation before a very exciting lightning round, I want to take us to failure corner. People listen to these podcast episodes and everyone's always just sharing all these wins, everything's always going great. The CPO of this, CPO of that, just moving on up and people will want to hear times when things didn't go right. Because those are stories people don't share as often. Can you share a story when something didn't go right, when you maybe had a failure in the course of your career? And if you learned something from that experience, what you learned.
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，在我们即将进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，我想先聊聊失败的角落。人们听这些播客节目时，总是在分享成功案例，一切都顺风顺水。某某公司的首席产品官，某某人事业蒸蒸日上，大家都想听听事情没那么顺利的时候的故事。因为这些故事不常被分享。你能分享一个自己职业生涯中失败的案例吗？如果从中吸取了教训，能讲讲是什么吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: I mean, there's a lot of things that didn't go exactly to plan, Lenny. Very early on in my career, I was still a developer and I accidentally deleted one of the core systems of the company that I was working at. So that's going to go down in infamy, but luckily that one's far in the rear-view mirror. That-
turns.zh: Lenny，我职业生涯早期遇到过很多事情没按计划进行的情况。我当时还是个开发者，误删了所在公司的核心系统。这事儿现在成了传奇，但好在已经过去很久了。那-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That wasn't Atlassian?
turns.zh: 那不是Atlassian吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: No, that was far pre-Atlassian, but very bad. Yeah, the one I like to talk about, I wasn't directly responsible for it, but I feel responsible for it. I was at a company and we launched a product. That was one of those products that in hindsight should have been really obvious it was going to fail, but for some reason we were all blinded by the potential. It was a product that was about, it was basically to measure the environmental impact of your company and to help you reduce the environmental impact of your company by doing, think about it as a power management, building power management, managing the power drawer of computers, managing the power drawer of AC and all of that stuff. That was the vision basically. It's like a manage your environmental impact of your business. The idea was pretty cool at the time, and also it was the right time for that, and it's still a thing. (01:09:33): It's still an area of active research and investment or whatever, but it was one of those things, talk about the wrong company, wrong place, wrong time, wrong distribution. We had literally no right to win, no right to play, just absolutely no business in hindsight being in that business. And I feel really bad because I, again, good idea, wrong company. And at the end of the day, we launched the product. We actually kept the product in market for two years, and the final straw was weird. The final straw was actually when a customer finally wanted to pay for it. It had been in market for two years, and we found ourselves with a customer who wanted to pay millions of dollars for it. They were ready to sign on the dotted line, and that was actually the moment we decided to kill the product because we were like, "If this person signs this piece of paper, we are stuck with this forever. This one customer will be bound by contracts for however long or whatever." (01:10:29): So we actually ended up killing it. At the moment after two years of failure when somebody wanted to pay his money for it. And I look back on that and I'm just like, "Man, that was a really big..." I feel really bad because I'm like, "It should have been obvious. It was obvious and we should have been able to call a spade a spade and I guess speak truth to power." But instead it kind of got through to the keeper and turned out to be a real accidental drain on resources for years and just a big mistake.
turns.zh: 不是，那是在加入Atlassian之前的事了，但情况很糟糕。是啊，我常提起的那次经历，虽然我不是直接负责人，却深感自责。当时我在一家公司推出一款产品。回过头看，这款产品注定失败，但当时我们却被潜力蒙蔽了双眼。这款产品的主旨是测量企业的环境影响，并通过节能管理来减少影响。具体来说，就好比电源管理——管理电脑的电源抽屉、管理交流电源等。这本该是个很有前景的项目。但时机、团队、资源统统不给力。（01:09:33）：如今这仍是活跃的研究与投资领域，但当时真是天时、地利、人和全都错了。我们根本没有胜算，注定要失败。事后看来，在那个时机、那个环境、那个公司里，根本不该做这件事。（01:10:29）：产品上线两年后，客户终于愿意付款，却成了压垮骆驼的最后一根稻草。客户愿意出几百万美元签约购买时，我们却选择了停掉项目。毕竟一旦签约，客户就被合同束缚住了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So is the lesson there, just be real with yourself? I like that you have this forcing function of like, "Okay, this is getting for real now." Is it like, "I wish we had an earlier forcing function to force us to make a decision?"
turns.zh: 所以教训就是，要对自己诚实吗？我欣赏你能设定一个强制函数，比如“好吧，现在真的到了关键时刻。”有没有希望能更早设定强制函数，迫使我们做出决策？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah. I think if I could do it differently, I might not have necessarily been able to 100% change the decision, but I should have tried. I mean, it was pretty obvious after six months, this thing was a bit of a zombie product walking, and the least I could have done is said, "This thing is dead." We could have called it dead way earlier, but instead we proceeded for another year and a half investing in it. And so that's the bit that makes me feel like real bummer about it.
turns.zh: 是啊。如果能重来，我或许无法百分百改变决策，但至少该尽力尝试。六个月后就明显看出产品像僵尸产品般苟延残喘，当时我至少该承认“这项目没戏了”。我们本可以更早放弃，却又投入了一年半的精力。这才是让我至今追悔莫及的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me a recent episode with Raaz who is the CMO at Wiz, and she joined us the first PM and a few weeks into it with doing tons of calls with customers she's like, "I think I need a quick... Because I don't really understand what we were building. I don't get it." And everyone's like, "I don't either." And it just, yeah, the founders just had a vague idea what they're doing, but they didn't really have an idea. And that just sparked a, "Okay, wait, no one actually does. Let's actually get more concrete." And it helped them pivot. And now, I don't know if you know about Wiz, but they ended up being the fastest growing startup in history.
turns.zh: 这让我想起最近与Wiz公司首席营销官Raaz的一次对话。她加入我们团队时，我们刚开始做首个产品发布会没几周，她就疯狂地给客户打电话。后来她说：“我觉得我需要快速了解一下……因为我真不明白我们在做什么产品。我完全摸不着头脑。”大家都说：“我也一样。”原来创始人们对产品的定位只是个模糊概念，根本没有清晰的思路。这次反思让大家意识到：“好吧，看来没人真正清楚状况。咱们得更具体化。”这最终帮助他们成功转型。不知道你是否了解Wiz公司，但它最终成为史上增长最快的初创企业。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yes. Isn't that amazing, right? It doesn't mean it's permanently fatal, but asking that question and going through that reckoning turns out that came out stronger.
turns.zh: 是啊。这难道不令人惊叹吗？这并不意味着失败是不可避免的，但提出这个问题并经历这样的反思，最终反而能让团队变得更强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Scary, but it turns out it's for the best often. Before we get to very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you want to mention or leave listeners with maybe a last nugget, something that you think might be helpful before we wrap?
turns.zh: 挺可怕的，但往往结果往往是好的。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你是否还有其他想和听众分享的见解，或者能在结束前给他们留下些启发的建议？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Maybe a couple of different things that I think are sometimes well understood, but just repeating them I guess because they're very valuable to me. One is that if you let your calendar rule you, then nothing good will happen. I know people talk about that a lot, but it's surprisingly common in product management in particular that people end up ruled by their calendar. And so it's related to that whole look at spend 80% of your time thinking about things going on outside the business. Easy said, very hard to do, and if you don't do it, no one's going to do it for you. And so it is really hard to be successful unless you find a way to force that to happen. So to repeat that, also, somebody said this to me, I never looked up the quote, but apparently Colin Powell said that if you're making a decision with less than 30% of the available data, you're making a big mistake. (01:13:32): If you're making a decision only after you have 70%, either the 70% or 77%, I can't remember the exact number, when you have 77% of all the available data, you have waited far too long. And I've always found that very insightful and it relates a little bit to what we're talking about about data earlier, but at the end of the day, we get paid in product management to make decisions, good decisions, paid to make good decisions that will deliver business benefit. And a decision with too little data is fatal. A decision that takes too long and collects too much data is also fatal. So everything, it's about trying to find the balance of all of these different things to try and deliver business advantage.
turns.zh: 或许有几个观点值得反复强调，虽然这些道理大家都懂，但对我来说却非常宝贵。第一，如果让日程表支配你的生活，就什么好事都做不成。我知道很多人常提这点，但在产品管理领域，人们被日程表支配的情况尤其常见。因此，关注外部事务需要投入80%的时间。这说起来容易做起来难，如果你不主动去做，就没人会替你完成。所以，除非你能找到强制执行的办法，否则很难成功。借用科林·鲍威尔的话：如果基于不到30%的可用数据做决策，那就是严重错误。（01:13:32）如果等到70%甚至77%数据才做决定，那就已经太晚了。这句话对我很有启发，也与我们之前讨论的数据相关。但归根结底，产品管理的核心是基于可用数据做出明智决策，创造商业价值。数据不足的决策是致命的，收集过多数据却拖延太久的决策同样致命。因此，关键在于平衡各方因素，创造商业价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A great way to circle back to all the things we've been talking about. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 这正好能回顾我们讨论过的所有内容。现在，激动人心的闪电问答环节开始了。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yes. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. What are two or three books that you have recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。你向他人推荐最多的三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, they oldies but goodies, is probably going to be The Lean Startup that I still find actually really good. And the key lessons in there I still think are very applicable to a lot of people, particularly the cohort analysis bit, which for some reason I still don't see people do anywhere near enough cohort analysis. So there you go, that's my little tip. And then INSPIRED: How to build products that people love by Marty Kagan and the Silicon Valley product group. That's an oldie but a goodie. I think it's got a lot of the key lessons of product management in it, even though it's been around for a long time.
turns.zh: 是啊，它们虽然是老书，但依然很棒。我觉得《精益创业》这本书至今仍非常不错。书中提到的关键经验至今仍适用于很多人，特别是关于用户群体分析的部分，不知为何，我发现现在很多人根本不做用户群体分析。好吧，这就是我的小建议。还有《灵感：如何打造人们喜爱的产品》这本书，作者是马蒂·卡根和硅谷产品团队。这也是一本经典之作。尽管它问世已久，但书中仍蕴含着产品管理的许多核心要义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Those are some classics. Very cool. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 这些都是经典之作。太棒了。你有没有特别喜欢的近期电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: I'm watching a program. I don't get to watch very much TV, mostly at night. I like to watch things that are extremely light, that just don't at all inspire any element of stress and that are very short. So basically short and funny is basically my thing. And there's a new program on Netflix, I think it's called Detroiters.
turns.zh: 我正在看一部节目。我不怎么看电视，大多是在晚上看。我喜欢看那种轻松愉快、完全不会带来压力而且时间很短的节目。所以简短有趣的节目基本上就是我的菜。Netflix上有一部新节目，好像叫《底特律人》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I've been watching that.
turns.zh: 哦，我一直在看这部剧。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, it's really funny. I really like that. It's so ridiculous, but very funny. So I like that.
turns.zh: 是啊，它真的很搞笑。我特别喜欢。剧情特别荒诞，但又特别有趣。所以我很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The main guy, he's so funny. I forget his name. Tim Sweeney or something like that. Yeah, he's so good. Good one. I've been watching that, I'm loving it. It's very quirky. I think the New York Times quote on there is "Very weird," the quote.
turns.zh: 主角特别有趣。我忘了他的名字。叫蒂姆·斯威尼之类的。是啊，他演得太棒了。真是个好节目。我一直在看，都爱上它了。它很古怪。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: It's so weird. In the first episode I'm like, "What is this show?" It's not even clear what time it set in, and it's very weird. It's really cool.
turns.zh: 太古怪了。第一集的时候我就在想，“这部剧讲什么啊？”连故事背景都说不清，特别奇怪。但真的很酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. Well, good way to describe it. Next question, do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 是啊，说得真贴切。下一个问题，你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, this one, some of your listeners might be using it, but Glean, it's a pretty well-known startup now. They recently raised a ton of money. We've been using Glean at Confluent for a long time and it's just amazing. It's just amazing. I can't describe how good it is. And I don't say this lightly because I think search, like business search is probably one of the hardest problems in computing. Actually getting it right is one of the hardest problems in computing. Amazing. It's not often I use a product and I'm like, "This thing is 10 times better than anything that's come before it." It's one of those for me.
turns.zh: 有啊，这个产品可能你们有些听众也在用，但Glean现在已经是个知名初创公司了。他们最近融资了大笔资金。我们在Confluent公司用Glean很久了，效果简直惊人。真的太棒了。我很少遇到一个产品让我觉得“它比之前的任何产品都好十倍”。对我来说，这款产品就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the simplest way to understand what it does for you?
turns.zh: 能简单解释一下它对你的帮助吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: It searches all of our organization's knowledge. So the thing you were just saying before, you're like, "What does AST mean?" If I had that in a meeting, I just open my new tab, it'll automatically take over my new tab or just like, "What does AST mean?" And it will summarize back to me what AST means and it'll give me a link to all the documents inside our company that just grab what AST means and then it will tell me who the expert in AST at our company is. It's like having a second brain. It's an insanely cool organization searching.
turns.zh: 它能搜索我们公司所有的知识库。比如你刚刚提到的“AST是什么意思？”如果我在会议上遇到这个问题，我只要打开新标签页，它就能自动替我搜索，或者直接输入“AST是什么意思？”它会给我总结AST的含义，还会链接到公司内所有提及AST的文档，甚至能告诉我公司里AST方面的专家是谁。简直就像个第二大脑。超酷的组织搜索工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great tip. Okay, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you come back to share with folks, find useful and work during life?
turns.zh: 好建议。好的，我还有两个问题。你有没有最喜欢的的人生格言，经常拿来与人分享、觉得很有用且能在生活中践行的？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: I think about this one a lot. When I started off in my career, I was an engineer's engineer. I used to very much about technical correctness and what computers were capable of, and technical righteousness, the right answer rather than there is only one right answer and whatever. It's a long-winded way of saying that I often think about this phrase, which is people don't care what you know until they know that you care. And so I've realized that really being able to influence people, it doesn't matter about whether or not you're right or whether or not you're wrong. And at the end of the day, it's first about trust and about relationships and caring about what each other's outcomes are, what their incentives are, and all good things sit on top of that. Once you have those kind of foundations, then you can build really good partnerships and that's where good progress comes from.
turns.zh: 我经常思考这个问题。刚开始职业生涯时，我是个技术宅，特别在意技术的正确性、计算机的能力极限，以及所谓的技术正义，认为只有一个正确答案之类的。说起来有点冗长，但我常想起这句话：人们在了解你关心他们之前，是不会在乎你的专业知识的。所以我意识到，真正影响他人并不取决于你是否正确，而是取决于信任、人际关系，以及对彼此结果的关心。只要建立了这些基础，就能建立良好的合作关系，进而取得真正的进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is so good. It connects with Radical Candor, similar in theory of just caring. People need to feel like you care deeply about them before they take your advice. And it also connects with this parenting book I'm reading called Listen, that a previous guest recommended, which is all about how your kids have problems when they feel like your connection to them is weak. And so the solution is to build a stronger connection for them to know that you cared deeply about them. So this is really, connected so much of what I've been reading.
turns.zh: 哇，太棒了。这和《激进坦诚》有共通之处，都是关于关心的理论。人们只有感受到你深切关怀，才会听取你的建议。这也和之前一位嘉宾推荐的育儿书《倾听》相呼应，书中指出，当孩子感觉与父母的联结薄弱时，他们就会出现问题。解决之道就是建立更深厚的联结，让他们知道你深切关心他们。所以这真的和我最近读的书有很多共鸣。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great one. Final question. You were born in Sydney, folks can maybe guess by your accent. If someone were to visit Sydney, any tips, anything you think they should check out, favorite thing in Sydney?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后一个问题。你出生在悉尼，听口音大家应该能猜到。如果有人去悉尼旅游，有什么建议吗？有什么必去的地方吗？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Yeah, Sydney is a really beautiful city and it's kind of famous for its beaches and it's basically a metropolitan city. People probably be very surprised when you visit it. It's a very big city, very metropolitan, a little bit like New York, but New York with really beautiful beaches, if you want to think about it that way, it's kind of crazy. But there's actually a ton of really cool nature and beautiful things all around Sydney. And so if you want to do something like off the beaten path, you can actually go to, there's an area called the Blue Mountains, which is like an hour and a half drive from Sydney, and you can abseil down a waterfall, which is, well actually firstly you go canyoning through a canyon full of water, and then you abseil off a waterfall at the end. And if you're looking for just a really beautiful, fun kind of adventure like thing, an hour and a bit away from a massive metropolitan city, that's my sort of happy place. Really beautiful outdoors stuff while also next to a beautiful city.
turns.zh: 是的，悉尼是个非常美丽的城市，以海滩闻名，基本上是个大都市。人们去那里旅游可能会大吃一惊。这是个大城市，非常繁华，有点像纽约，但纽约有美丽的海滩，如果你这么想的话，就很疯狂了。不过悉尼周边其实有很多很棒的自然景观和美景。所以如果你想寻找一些与众不同的体验，可以去蓝山地区，距离悉尼车程一个半小时，在那里可以沿着满是水流的峡谷徒步，然后从瀑布上速降。或者如果你想找个既有美丽户外风光又毗邻大都市的地方，那就是我的快乐之地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you said you sail, what sort of sail off a waterfall?
turns.zh: 你说你会速降，从瀑布上下来？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Abseil. You might think of it as rappelling. Rappelling, I think. Yeah, lowering yourself down on a rope or...
turns.zh: 速降。你可能把它和 rappelling 混淆了。是 rappelling。我觉得是这样。用绳子把自己降下悬崖，或者……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Because when I hear sail, I'm thinking a boat just jumps through over the waterfall.
turns.zh: 明白了。因为我一听到“速降”，就以为是船只从瀑布上飞跃过去。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Oh, no, abseiling which is also, I think in the States you guys call it rappelling.
turns.zh: 哦，不，速降，我想在美国你们管它叫 rappelling。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Rappelling, yeah. Wow. Very cool. Shaun, you're awesome. This was extremely cool. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out? Also point folks to your Reforge courses that you created. And final question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 速降，对呀。哇。太酷了。肖恩，你太棒了。这真是太酷了。非常感谢你能来参加节目。最后两个问题。如果大家想联系你，应该去哪里找你？另外请帮我们宣传一下你创建的 Reforge 课程。最后一个问题，听众们怎样才能为你提供帮助呢？

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Sure. Yeah, so my Reforge courses, you can check them all out at reforge.com, as you mentioned, the retention, engagement course and the data for product managers course, so love to see folks get some value from that. Lots of people have been through those courses already and I really get a lot of value from it because like I said, one of my goals is to help all of us be better product people. I think our leverage could be massive. Where you can get in touch with me, obviously on LinkedIn, but also ShaunMClowes on X, if you want to get in touch. And in terms of being useful to me, I mean, broadly speaking, I'm always open to new ideas. If people have ideas about how to do better B2B, PLG, better B2B product-led sales, for example, better ways of going about distribution and product-led sales and product-led growth inside enterprise companies, hey, I'm open to learn myself. We're all in one big journey learning how to do this better.
turns.zh: 好的。是的，我的 Reforge 课程，你可以在 reforge.com 上查看所有课程，正如你提到的，包括用户留存与互动课程，以及产品经理数据分析课程。我很希望大家能从中获得价值。已经有很多学员完成了这些课程，我自己也从中收获了很多，因为正如我所说，我的目标之一就是帮助我们所有人成为更出色的产品经理。我认为我们能产生巨大的影响力。想联系我的话，显然可以通过领英，但也可以在 X 平台上搜索 ShaunMClowes。如果想为我提供帮助，广义上来说，我一直乐于接受新想法。比如，如果大家对如何提升 B2B 业务、PLG（产品生命周期管理）、B2B 产品主导型销售，或者如何在企业内部推动分销和产品主导型增长有好的建议，我都非常欢迎学习。毕竟我们都在不断探索如何把这些做得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So true. Shaun, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太对了。肖恩，非常感谢你能来参加节目。

turns.speaker: Shaun Clowes
turns.en: Awesome, thank you very much, Lenny. It was great.
turns.zh: 太棒了，非常感谢，莱尼。这次交流很棒。
